Bergeret considers a possible misuse or misconstrual of dreams in the course of psychoanalytic work. It is not simply a matter of stratifying a dream into manifest and latent contents. We should be open to the plurality of levels from which a dream issues. The author recalls Freud's thesis of a primary unconscious, an unconscious which never underwent repression, and also his thesis about a "fundamental language." On this latter level one must listen not only for traces of infantile affective life, but, in addition, for a mode of thought which is more archaic and primitive. Some pathways in a dream may descend into this archaic level. Bergeret makes some suggestions on correlating dreams with recent neurophysiological studies. He suggests that the basic dream activity is contemporaneous with deep sleep. The dream images are synchronous with the paradoxical EEG phase. Representations from the primary unconscious become veritable images attached to word-presentations, eye movements, pressure and pulse at the end of the paradoxical phase. [[RunningHead]]

American Journal of Psychiatry. CXXXV, 1978

Is Modern-Day Schizophrenic Outcome Still Negative? Martin Harrow, et al. Pp. 1156-1162.

To evaluate formulations about more positive outcome in modern-day schizophrenic patients, the authors assessed 132 young patients 2.7 years after hospital discharge. Despite modern treatment techniques, only 14%-17% of the 79 schizophrenic patients in the study group were functioning effectively without relapses; 50% had adjusted very poorly. The schizophrenic patients were functioning significantly more poorly than the nonschizophrenic patients in all areas (p < .01), showing poor adjustment, high symptom levels, and high rehospitalization rates. The two major acute subgroups (schizoaffective and acute schizophrenic patients) were functioning better than those with paranoid and chronic schizophrenia. Overall, the authors conclude, diagnosis carries prognostic implications. Schizophrenic outcome is more favorable today than it was in Bleuler and Kraepelin's era, but it is still relatively negative.

Lowell Rubin

Lowell Rubin  

A case report is given of the psychological response to testicular implant in a thirty-year-old man. The patient was articulate and able to report fantasy material that was analytic in quality. Reports are detailed from before the surgery, at the time of surgery, and ten months and three years later. Unfortunately, the nature of the therapeutic contact is not made clear. The report is significant in that it provides greater insight into the psychological meaning of surgical procedure, demonstrates the importance of anatomical abnormalities for the development of identity and overall functioning, and stresses the importance of psychological questions in relation to procedures that alter body image.

The Psychohistory Review. VII, No. 2, 1979

Heinz Kohut and the Historical Imagination. Charles B. Strozier. Pp. 36-39.

Peter Buckley

Peter Buckley

Peter Buckley  

The author advocates the inclusion of Kohut's theoretical formulations on the psychology of the self into psychohistorical studies. Kohut's own work has provided psychobiographical vignettes of Hitler and Churchill which emphasize the interplay between the grandiose self, the ego, and the superego in determining adult personality. Kohut sees Hitler as having had a "healed-over psychosis" in which he retained the ability to test reality but in which his reasoning capacity entirely served his rigid narcissistic personality structure. Kohut has also commented on Hitler's ability to subordinate others to his grandiose fantasies of magical-sadistic control over the whole world. The author of this review essay feels that psychohistorians are faced with the urgent need to apply Kohut's psychology of the self to their work.

Journal of Psycholinguistic Research. VII, 1978

Some Psychological Relations Between Action and Language Structure. Patricia Marks Greenfield and Michael A. Westerman. Pp. 453-475.

This study investigated the relationship between complex grammatical structures and complex action sequences. A developmental progression of strategies for combining seriated cups identified in an earlier study was used to demonstrate some psychological consequences of formal parallels between language and action. The role of grammatical complexity and situational structure in language-action relations was explored. The results have implications for understanding the organization and development of complex action, its control by verbal commands, and the basic processes of speech comprehension.

American Journal of Psychiatry. CXXXV, 1978

An Alternative View of the Neurobiology of Dreaming. Gerald W. Vogel. Pp. 1531-1535.

A critique of the recently proposed activation-synthesis hypothesis on the origin and formation of dreams is presented. Many findings do not support the new hypothesis that specific pontine physiological processes, rather than mental processes, instigate dreams and produce their distortion. First, dreaming often occurs in the absence of the pontine processes. Second, forebrain activity (which can have mental correlates) is crucial to the instigation and maintenance of dreaming sleep. Finally, activity of the proposed pontine dream generator, which is claimed to cause dream distortion, is not reliably accompanied by dream distortion.

Symbol and Neurosis. Selected Papers of Lawrence S. Kubie. (Psychological Issues, Monograph 44.)

Edited by Herbert J. Schlesinger. New York: International Universities Press, Inc., 1978. 277 pp.

Peter Richter

Peter Richter

Peter Richter
NEW YORK

Peter Richter  

Many young analysts may be quite unfamiliar with Lawrence Kubie's scientific writings and unaware of the influential role he played during the formative years of psychoanalysis in this country. Although one senses that his direct influence began to recede before his death in 1973, his indirect influence is very much alive—for example, the current experimental program for training a small group of nonmedical analysts at the University of California is based in large part upon ideas Kubie espoused during his lifetime.

Kubie belonged to the first generation of American analysts (if one looks upon the earliest group as "analytic pioneers"), many of whom came to analysis after training in other medical specialties. Often they went abroad for what one would now regard as brief analyses and didactic training. (Kubie went to England.) Their diverse interests and talents brought a vigor and color to the analytic movement which is missed. Kubie's interests were almost boundless. A hasty perusal of the bibliography of Symbol and Neurosis, which includes only a sampling of his more than three hundred published writings, demonstrates clearly his remarkably broad range of interests: hypnosis, sensory deprivation, combat exhaustion, the implications of transsexual surgery, the relation of art to psychotherapy, a critical review of the Kinsey Report, and his introduction to the publication of Moss Hart's Lady in the Dark. His references to the works of others are correspondingly broad, covering, in addition to psychoanalytic writings, the fields of psychiatry, neurophysiology, psychobiology, the arts and social sciences, to name but a few. Probably no analyst contributed as many articles to as diverse a range of publications as Lawrence Kubie—from The Psychoanalytic Quarterly to the Saturday Evening Post.

Heinz Lichtenstein  

While Charles W. Socarides may be best known for his theoretical and clinical work in the field of sexual perversions, it would be doing him an injustice to evaluate his contributions solely in terms of his psychoanalytic work. He has long been known for his great personal and moral courage in standing up for his convictions, even when this has meant considerable personal risk. As a social thinker, he has not hesitated to offer criticism of popular trends of thought whenever he felt such trends were not in the public interest. Beyond Sexual Freedom shows him in the role of social critic, and his critique is often quite acerbic. I believe, however, that it would be an underestimation of the true value of his book to see it primarily as a polemic on problems of sexuality as the author sees them manifest in promiscuity, homosexuality, pornography, feminism, and the modern state of marriage and family life. The book has a more profound motivation: underlying all Socarides's combativeness there is genuine doubt about, perhaps despair over, the possibility of a future for mankind, for Western civilization, and for American civilization in particular.

Socarides is one of those who have been voicing intellectual concern about what has been called the "New America." These distressing doubts we find expressed in many poignant statements of our best literary commentators. Socarides's views belong, for example, in the context of the following statement by Elizabeth Hardwick:

Only the forgetful can easily ignore the duplicity practiced upon the defining imagination by the sudden obsolescence of attitudes and styles just past… These elements … had the shape of reality, of historical presence … and even though they could not be asserted as eternal they still could not be experienced as mere historical moments soon, very soon, to be

This work by Lasch is an ambitious, always thoughtful, and at times brilliant delineation of a half-century of thought about a subject of great interest to psychoanalysts: the family. The book, an intellectual history, surveys American family studies by social scientists from the early twenties to the present. Lasch feels that the American tradition of family study has limited itself through its neglect of psychoanalytic concepts. He feels further that these studies, through their influence upon social workers, marriage counselors, and others, have contributed to the demise of the family in American society.

Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XXXIX, 1975

The Lost Object—the Self. Notes on Endocryptic Identification. Nicolas Abraham and Maria Torok. Pp. 409-426.

The authors describe a specific mechanism of identification which they designate as "endocryptic." The individual identifies not just with an object, but comes to express the imagined sufferings of that object. The object is "entombed" in a psychic crypt, as it were, in an effort to mask the real and unresolved trauma created by its loss. The authors suggest this specific mechanism is an important one for the understanding of the fantasy life of many melancholics. They offer clinical examples from their own cases and claim, too, that the "secret" of the Wolf Man involved not just the memory of being seduced by his sister, but also an earlier seduction of the sister by their father. The authors suggest techniques for dealing with the opening of the endopsychic crypt in the course of therapy and the reintegration of the libidinal attitudes toward the lost object.

170

Adolescent Psychiatry: Developmental and Clinical Studies. V, 1977

Parents and Adolescents: Empathy and the Vicissitudes of Development. Andre P. Derdeyn and David B. Waters. Pp. 175-185.

The "empathy" in question is that of the therapist for the parents of the adolescent in treatment, as well as empathy or lack of it in communication between adolescents and their parents as they traverse the difficult period of mutual separation. If the therapist focuses with the adolescent patient only on issues of freedom and independence and neglects to deal also with the need to reach toward empathy with and acceptance of parents as people, the patient is shortchanged. In remembering the developmental needs of the parents, the therapist of their adolescent child may also be in the position to guide them toward help they may need in mastering this phase of psychological development in themselves.

Adolescent Psychiatry: Developmental and Clinical Studies. V, 1977

The "Juvenile Impostor": Some Thoughts on Narcissism and the Delinquent. Richard C. Marohn. Pp. 186-212.

The author, referring to techniques and theoretical formulations developed by A. Aichhorn and H. Kohut, offers case histories of several delinquent teenagers treated as inpatients at a research unit of the Illinois State Psychiatric Institute. He then discusses the cases, focusing on disturbances in the development of narcissism in these patients. He views their grandiose, manipulative behavior as defense against fragmentation of fragile egos; as defensive regression to a period of early pathological fixation when impulse and action, self and nonself are undifferentiated. He describes the difficulties of analytic treatment with adolescents who seek omnipotence in the same therapist whom they relentlessly attempt to deceive.

174

Adolescent Psychiatry: Developmental and Clinical Studies. V, 1977

Narcissistic Disturbances in Anorexia Nervosa. Alan Goodsitt. Pp. 304-312.

In a paper which beautifully complements and elaborates on the preceding one by Bruch, anorexia nervosa is presented as a form of narcissistic personality disorder or "borderline psychosis." There has been early failure in establishment of a cohesive sense of self. In the face of the usual developmental tasks initiated at puberty, the anorectic establishes the typical symptomatic picture of extreme, concrete efforts to control body and environment in an attempt to avert a sense of emptiness and fragmentation. The author believes that behavior modification can be destructive in ignoring the patient's potential for individuation; he strongly advocates a slow, careful psychoanalytic approach similar to that espoused by Bruch.

175

Adolescent Psychiatry: Developmental and Clinical Studies. V, 1977

Termination of Treatment in Adolescence. Jack Novick. Pp. 390-412.

In this superb paper the following important issues are discussed, with material from the analysis of an adolescent boy as illustration. (1) Adolescents often enter analysis with an overt or covert plan for unilateral termination early in treatment. For analysis truly to begin, the patient must at some point be confronted with the need to relinquish this plan. (2) Criteria for the beginning of the terminal phase are discussed. The start must be a mutual recognition, rather than a decision, and, in the adolescent, is initiated by the patient's ability to experience and maintain in the transference an oedipal level of psychic organization. (3) Because "termination" of childhood relationships with parents is a crucial task of adolescence, the technique of initiation of termination is crucial in adolescent analysis. The topic should be broached and the date set by the adolescent, and the date (remaining unaltered once set) should occur at a time when the analyst is working rather than during a holiday. (4)

[[RunningHead]]

The History of Childhood

Edited by Lloyd DeMause. New York: The Psychohistory Press, 1974. 450 pp.

Alan Zients

Alan Zients

Alan B. Zients
WASHINGTON, D.C.

Alan Zients  

The ten psychohistorians contributing to this scholarly volume have presented us with a survey of childhood in the Western world from 200 A.D. to the nineteenth century. Recognizing the nuclear significance of the first years of life and the paucity of relevant historical research, they collated widely diverse source material in their reconstruction of the ways of interaction of different generations of parents and children. This ambitious undertaking was the result of five years of research sponsored by the Association for Applied Psychoanalysis.

In the first chapter, the editor, Lloyd DeMause, outlines his "psychogenic theory" of history, asserting that the central force for change is neither technology nor economics, but "the psychogenic changes in personality occurring because of successive generations of parent-child interactions" (p. 3). Psychic structure is passed from generation to generation through the narrow funnel of childhood.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Whispered Meanings. Selected Essays of Simon O. Lesser

Edited by Robert Sprich and Richard W. Noland. Amherst, Mass.: The University of Massachusetts Press, 1977. 250 pp.

Meredith Skura

Meredith Skura

Meredith Skura
HOUSTON

Meredith Skura  

In The Whispered Meanings Robert Sprich and Richard Noland have collected fourteen of Simon Lesser's essays on "fiction," ranging in genre and period from Greek epic and drama (the Odyssey and Oedipus the King), to Shakespearean drama (Hamlet, Lear, and Macbeth), to eighteenth and nineteenth century novels and short stories (by Fielding, Hawthorne, Flaubert, and Dostoevsky), to Yeats's lyrics ("Sailing to Byzantium"), to contemporary drama (Pinter's Birthday Party) and film (Antonioni's L'Avventura). The essays are based on and frequently recapitulate assumptions which Lesser had outlined in his Fiction and the Unconscious.1 That by now classic theoretical work had brought the insights of ego psychology to bear on Freud's earlier discoveries about fantasy and wish fulfillment and had served also as a practical guide both sane and provocative, applying psychoanalytic insights with Lesser's rare sensitivity to the actual details of texts. The book has served as the starting point for psychoanalytic literary criticism ever since.

The essays in Whispered Meanings re-emphasize Lesser's earlier theory as they provide new applications. As always, Lesser reminds us of the multiplicity of meanings in a work, concerning himself in particular with those meanings which, he always felt, have been ignored by general readers and literary critics—the unconsciously perceived or "whispered" meanings. These are the ones, as Lesser defines them, which deal with and work out psychic conflicts. ("Fiction ventilates our conflicts … brings all the claims out into the open … [and] seeks actively to reconcile them" [p. 33]. Lesser makes this point explicitly in the one theoretical essay in the collection, "The Attitude of Fiction," but it is implicit in all the essays.)

1Lesser, S. O.: Fiction and the Unconscious. Boston: The Beacon Press, 1957. Reviewed in This QUARTERLY, XXVII, 1958, pp. 270-271.330

[[RunningHead]]

Bulletin of the Menninger Clinic. XLI, 1977

On the Psychotherapy of Patients with Anorexia Nervosa. Helmut Thomä. Pp. 437-452.

In some cases of anorexia nervosa, tube feeding is the only "psychosomatic" means to break through the vicious cycle of illness, but even this must be approached psychotherapeutically. The loss of weight and the accompanying somatic symptoms do not correlate with the seriousness of the psychopathological syndrome. According to Anna Freud, the self-starvation is one expression of "asceticism at puberty" with illusory wish fulfillment. Oral incorporation becomes a prototype of object finding. Sexual fears are displaced onto the body as a whole with delusional ego distortions. Ambivalent relationships to the mother are marked by severe libidinal and ego regressions. In applying these psychodynamics to treatment, Thomä uses psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapy. The greatest problem lies in establishing a working alliance. The most important consideration is to avoid collusion with the patient's denial of reality, and at times the patient must be treated in a hospital. Defenses must be challenged, not glossed over. Because these patients reject physicians' recommendations, marked countertransference attitudes are aroused.

335

Bulletin of the Menninger Clinic. XLII, 1978

The Conceptualization of the Therapeutic Action of Psychoanalysis: The Action of the Holding Environment. Arnold Modell. Pp. 493-504.

S. Seides

S. Seides

S. Seides  

Because of the increase in frequency of the analyses of narcissistic disorders, Modell has drawn attention to the development of the actual object relationship to the analyst as the locus of the therapeutic action in these cases. In this interplay the analyst can be said to be symbolically "holding" the patient. This is analogous to holding a child who is having a temper tantrum or communicating to an adult that he cannot destroy the analyst with his sadism. It provides a measure of actual gratification, especially during the early phases of the analysis of certain narcissistic character disorders when there exists a persistent state of affective nonrelatedness. For these patients the analytic setting and procedure themselves become the focus of their conflicts. The lack of a full sense of separateness from others causes these patients to accept empathic interpretations only if they support the illusion of fusion with the analyst, not for their content. The illusion of merging with an impotent analyst needs to be analyzed in order to touch the core of the neurosis.

337

Psychoanalytic Study of the Child. XXXII, 1977

Fears, Anxieties, and Phobic Phenomena. Anna Freud. Pp. 85-90.

In her usual crisp and lucid style Anna Freud offers a brief commentary on the papers and discussions of the Association for Child Psychoanalysis meeting in London, July 1976. She deals instructively with anxiety and phobia and challenges the view that the phobic object has a compelling attraction for the child. Clinical evidence demonstrates that the true phobic defense is effective in blotting out any seductive qualities concealed in the anxiety, leaving the child truly calm in the absence of the phobic object. Both neurotic symptoms and healthy character formation require the same unpleasant affects for their development. Where, then, is the dividing line between the positive and negative impacts of fear and anxiety? Does it relate to quantitative factors, qualitative factors, and/or timing in their arrival on the developmental path?

339

[[RunningHead]]

Psychoanalytic Study of the Child. XXXII, 1977

Narcissism as a Function of Culture. Simon Sobo. Pp. 155-172.

Alice Frankel

Alice Frankel

Alice Frankel  

The increased prevalence of narcissistic difficulties in the United States is the result of the cultural shifts and upheavals of the 1960's and the early 1970's. The "remarkable" attack on authorities and values favored the dissolution of the superego with a resultant greater reliance on the ego ideal. Sobo uses superego in the restricted sense of the oedipal prohibitor, and ego ideal in the sense of the preoedipal wish-fulfilling agency. Later in the paper he links the former to identification with the oedipal father and the latter to identification with the preoedipal mother (he also states this refers to boys only). A reciprocal relationship between the two is posited: as the superego standards relax, the ego ideal wishes are unleashed. Conversely, the more the yearnings of the ego ideal are fulfilled, the more the superego restrictions are relaxed. As examples of this he cites romantic love and group behaviors. His main point is that the establishment of the superego as authority (a product of the oedipus complex via identification with the father-aggressor) requires, for most people, continuing reinforcement throughout life, but especially in adolescence. The disintegration of institutions and community in the 1960's made this reinforcement impossible. Society no longer provided the effective symbolic father.

340

[[RunningHead]]

American Imago. XXXV, 1978

Vaslav Nijinsky: Genius and Schizophrenic. Anne Wilson Wangh. Pp. 221-237.

When Nijinsky was five years old, his father, a dancer, abandoned him along with his mother, his older brother, and his younger sister. Shortly thereafter his brother was left mentally incapacitated after falling out of a window; thus Nijinsky became "the man of the house" at the height of his oedipal period. A year or two later his father, who returned from time to time, threw Nijinsky into the Neva in an attempt to teach him to swim; he had to be rescued by other swimmers. These events helped form his passive, fearful personality. Three months after his graduation, at age eighteen, from the Imperial School of Ballet, Nijinsky met and became the lover of Diaghilev, the impressario under whom he achieved international fame. At the age of twenty-three, while on a tour of South America, Nijinsky married Romola, a beautiful Hungarian girl who had talked her way into the company. Diaghilev was furious and soon found an excuse to dismiss Nijinsky, whereupon the latter's career and mental stability began to falter. He never danced again after giving a concert he called "Marriage with God" at the age of twenty-nine; this was a psychotic performance and he was soon thereafter declared incurably insane by Bleuler.

340

Psychiatrica Fennica (Finnish Psychiatry). 1978

On the Ethical Problem of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy. Kalle Achté. Pp. 153-161.

Owen Renik

Owen Renik

Owen Renik  

Achté briefly and candidly reviews a variety of ethical issues inherent in psychiatric treatment, sometimes giving his own impressions, but generally avoiding the tendency to reach for premature closure. The difficulties therapists have in acknowledging their own limitations are discussed, as well as the temptation to intervene in a patient's life or, on the contrary, to adhere to a rigid, mechanical view of psychotherapy. Achté touches on the particular ethical hazards in group therapy and behavioral techniques. He considers the dilemma of involuntary treatment and the question of the right to suicide. These various themes are drawn together in a section on the need for study of the therapeutic process. Finally, connection is made to the general topic of the ethics of science.

342

Psychiatrica Fennica Supplementum. 1978

On Some Narcissistic Aspects of Self-Destructive Behavior and Their Influence on Its Predictability. Veikko A. Tähkä. Pp. 59-62.

Owen Renik

Owen Renik

Owen Renik  

Tähkä considers cases of suicides which came as a surprise to the therapist. He suggests that in these instances the narcissistic regression characterizing depression is so extreme that the patient's most important feelings are directed almost totally toward internal objects. As a result, the therapist does not receive those emotional signals that ordinarily induce countertransferences and provide the information from which alarm about the patient's condition would arise. Tähkä suggests, as a practical matter, that a therapist should be on the alert when he or she notices the absence of emotional concern toward a depressed patient. He also suggests that referring to such feelings in the therapist as "complementary reactions," rather than as countertransferences, would be more accurate and would facilitate clarity about their use in the treatment situation.

[[RunningHead]]

Journal of Youth and Adolescence. VII, 1978

Death Fantasies of Father-Absent and Father-Present Late Adolescents. Harvey P. Oshman and Martin Manosevitz. Pp. 41-48.

Parental perceptions of father-absent and father-present late adolescents were studied by having them create stories to selected pictures from the Thematic Apperception Test and the Michigan Pictures Test. Ratings on the manifest thematic content of the stories revealed that father-present females, but not males, introduced themes of death and loss involving the parents with significantly greater frequency than did late adolescents who had actually lost their fathers. One of the tasks of adolescence, as described in psychoanalytic writings, is decathecting internalized parental images. It is possible that father-present females produced significantly more death and loss themes because they were actively coping with their fantasies of parental loss. The significantly fewer fantasies of parental loss given by father-absent females is consistent with this psychoanalytic model which suggests that the loss of a parent at an earlier developmental period complicates the decathexis process in adolescence. Reasons for the failure to find differences between father-absent and father-present males are discussed, and suggestions for future research are provided.

James Bernard

James Bernard

James Bernard  

DISCUSSION: Dr. Aaron H. Esman felt that the acquisition of abstract conceptual thought, as described by Piaget, is instrumental in the revision of ego ideal and superego standards during adolescence. The reference to Mahler's work in Blos's discussion of a second individuation phase is an important analogy and can be extended even further to subphase parallels. Dr. Esman stated his belief that major regression in adolescence is not as ubiquitous as generally thought. What is essential for the adolescent is an openness to the possibility of regression and the absence of a premature closure of possibilities. Dr. Peter B. Neubauer said that Dr. Blos's outstanding application of the developmental point of view to adolescence offers a challenge to the recapitulation theory. Adolescence is not only a new phase organization which permits different solutions to earlier problems, but a phase in which there are new and specific tasks.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Freud, Biologist of the Mind. Beyond the Psychoanalytic Legend

By Frank J. Sulloway. New York: Basic Books, Inc., 1979. 612 pp.

Mark Kanzer

Mark Kanzer

Mark Kanzer
HARRISON, N.Y.

Mark Kanzer  

In this book Frank Sulloway calls for multiple revisions of established views on Freud and psychoanalysis, views which, he declares, are wrapped in myths and politics. His own thesis may well be best set forth in the title, Freud, Biologist of the Mind, and the subtitle, Beyond the Psychoanalytic Legend. Describing his study as a "comprehensive intellectual biography of Sigmund Freud," he considers that it offers a scientific approach in contrast to the usual type of scholarship seen up to now. This, he claims, "has been a largely internal affair dominated by Freud, the Freud family, psychoanalysts-turned-historians, and former patients. Over the years these psychoanalytic devotees have cultivated a complex and politically expedient mythology about their collective past, a mythology that ranks as a fascinating accomplishment in its own right" (p. xiii). Presumably no conditions were laid down to insure Sulloway's adherence to a particular political mythology, since he speaks of his research at the Freud library in England where "Dr. Anna Freud kindly allowed me to examine [a] portion of her father's personal library" and extended "gracious hospitality during my several visits to the Freud home" (p. xvii).

The author's background includes a period as a junior fellow in the Harvard Society of Fellows, at which time he wrote this book, and later membership in the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton. At last report, he occupied a postdoctoral fellowship in psychology at the University of California, Berkeley. The jacket assures us that "this revealing work completely transforms our understanding of Freud. After reading it, no one will ever see the man or his work in the same light again." The advertising for this book has been vigorous and in the same vein, and an expectable following among reviewers has jubilantly taken up the cry. Nevertheless, there have been several reservations and expressions of criticism as well.

Sulloway's approach is challenging and fervid throughout the closely packed volume, justifying the jacket claims that it is "brilliantly written and meticulously researched.

The Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis: From 1932 to the Present. George H. Pollock. Pp. 3-22.

James Bing

James Bing

James Bing  

The Chicago Institute was to a large extent modeled by Alexander on the Berlin Institute. This article, however, is perhaps more noteworthy for its contribution to the history of psychoanalysis than for its discussion of the history of the development of the Chicago Institute. For example, Hans Sachs was the first training analyst. He became a training analyst for what was known at the time as the Berlin Psychoanalytic Society, founded by Karl Abraham in 1908, but it was not until 1923 or 1924 that it became an official training center. The word "institute" was first used at a meeting of the Berlin Psychoanalytic Society in 1922, and the Vienna Society opened its Institute three years later in 1925. Many other well-known psychoanalysts are discussed in this article. The Chicago Institute built its experience upon its heritage from Vienna and Berlin and over the years widely extended its influence by sponsoring institutes in other areas: Topeka, Detroit, Cincinnati, Denver, and St. Louis.

International Journal of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy. VII, 1978-1979

Introjection and the Idealizing Transference. Theodore C. Dorpat. Pp. 23-53.

Owen Renik

Owen Renik

Owen Renik  

A case report in which the patient idealized her analyst is used to explicate a two-step process: first, introjection, defined as a replication in fantasy of relations with a real object, i.e., the analyst; then identification, in which aspects of the introjected object are taken over as part of the self. The need to permit idealization of the analyst for this purpose, rather than to interfere with idealization by "reality testing," is emphasized. Deferred imitation refers to the repetition of perceived interchanges with the analyst post-facto outside the hours. Deferred imitation is an important manifestation of introjection.

The author agrees with Dorpat's view, but prefers the term functional introject because specific functions of the analyst, rather than his person, are at issue. For introjection to occur, a boundary between self and object must be established in the patient's mind. Prior to that, preintrojective use of the analyst as a transitional object may be necessary. A case example is given in which countertransference reactions and resulting misinterpretations are seen as having usefully facilitated such a process.

For its historical interest, Searles publishes here the first article he ever wrote about psychiatry, which was submitted to and turned down by two journals in 1949. In it, he speaks of transference as based on projections by the patient, but projections which have a kernel of truth, in that they take account of actual qualities in the therapist. His aim was to discourage the tendency in beginning therapists to aspire toward an image of themselves as emotionally uninvolved in their treatments. Countertransferences need to be acknowledged by the therapist, especially when they correspond to patients' transference projections. This is an inevitable and important aspect of any psychoanalytic treatment.

November 28, 1978. THE RONDANINI PIETÀ. MICHELANGELO'S INFANTILE NEUROSIS. (Abraham A. Brill Memorial Lecture.) Andrew Peto, M.D.

Michelangelo's last sculptured work was the Rondanini Pietà which is now in Milan. Dr. Peto proposed that the three stages through which this work is believed to have evolved represent attempts at a creative solution of Michelangelo's most basic conflict—wishing to be united with his mother in eternal love while at the same time fighting against annihilating fusion with her. Dr. Peto related the intensity of this central conflict to two features of the artist's early life: 1) shortly after his birth he had been sent away to a wet nurse, the wife of a stone cutter on the small Buonarroti farm outside Florence; and 2) his mother had died when he was six years old. Drawing upon a statement attributed to Michelangelo by his contemporary biographer, Condivi, in which the artist claimed that his capacity as a sculptor was transmitted through the power of the milk of the stone cutter's wife, Dr. Peto emphasized the important role of the wet nurse in Michelangelo's development. He speculated that a major traumatic aspect of the boy's situation was his mother's frequent visits to the family farm and her abrupt departures. (The length of Michelangelo's stay with the stone cutter's family is not actually known. Dr. Peto, however, assumed that the artist remained as a foster child until age ten.) Thus, the experience of being abandoned over and over again left Michelangelo in a state of insecurity, rage, and depression: each visit must have raised his hopes that the family would take him back to Florence with them; every new abandonment must have increased his feelings of hopelessness and helplessness. Out of this childhood situation developed Michelangelo's basic depressive mood, which was expressed in many of his works and reached its pinnacle in the Rondanini Pietà.

Dr. Peto regards the Rondanini Pietà as the last phase in the artist's unresolved conflict over his relationship with his mother. An earlier phase was the eight years of work on the Pietà that is now in Florence Cathedral. Dr. Peto drew upon art historian Tolnay's description of the Florence Pietà: "The individual bodies are fused; they merge with one another and are united like their feelings. Each figure is but a nuance of the beatitude which results from participation in divine love." In the Florence Pietà Jesus and Mary are brought together by a figure that represents either Nicodemus or Joseph of Arimathea, a figure that is also Michelangelo's self-portrait. Peto, citing Michelangelo's childhood confusion over his actual father and the stone cutter surrogate, assumed that the figure was intended to be Joseph—also the name of Mary's husband, who was not the father of Christ. Thus, Joseph of Arimathea mirrors the confused inner representation of "father" on the part of Michelangelo.

We seem to be making some headway in the treatment of "borderlines." For the more disturbed segment of this population, programs of individual, group, and family therapy in residential or transitional settings (i.e., group homes) offer some hope of a life that may be productive and during which only periodic hospitalization is

707

necessary. If these patients live in the right "catchment area" or if they have enough money, the various treatment approaches are coordinated, focused, and informed by a continuing relationship with an empathic, trained professional. In spite of the fact that in both public and private organizations the least experienced individuals tend to see the most difficult cases, some psychoanalysts do work with this kind of patient. In addition, they supervise and train many of the other professionals who do this work, and through such teachers many of the recent reformulations of narcissism, object relations theory, and psychoanalytic research on early development have infused the training programs.

Developing a capacity for accurate empathic perception and response is the core task for trainees in the mental health field. Contributors to the psychoanalytic literature on borderlines and the narcissistic disorders have provided a theoretical substructure that has helped to refine empathic skills. Many in the field suggest that if therapists can tune in to patients' perceptions and to their affective responses to the world, a relationship is possible which can provide a foundation for progressive personal development through the reopening of the developmental dialogue and later through interpretive work.

The theoretical contributions referred to have provided some rudimentary conceptual tools to those who struggle with the management of very disturbed patients, tools that are mainly effective in the understanding and control of countertransference hate, and they have enriched our understanding of the "more or less analyzable" patient whose preoedipal concerns require an empathic analyst as a continuing precondition for interpretive work. Unfortunately, these two levels of contribution tend to be blurred by the tempting notion that our patients and our techniques can be arranged along a developmental continuum.

Withdrawal symptoms frequently follow abrupt discontinuation of antipsychotic compounds. In addition to other somatic symptoms, withdrawal-emergent dyskinesias may be observed. "Covert dyskinesia" refers to a masked form of tardive dyskinesia that becomes clinically detectable only after antipsychotic drugs are withdrawn or their dosage is reduced. Withdrawal dyskinesia appears under similar circumstances but disappears spontaneously in six to twelve weeks. Cholinergic overactivity and changes in dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the basal ganglia may underlie these withdrawal syndromes. The principal value of the concept of covert dyskinesia is in the secondary and tertiary prevention of tardive dyskinesia through early discovery and treatment.

Meetings of the Psychoanalytic Association of New York

Joel Gonchar

Joel Gonchar

Joel Gonchar  

February 26, 1979. ON ASPECTS OF COUNTERTRANSFERENCE IN TREATING THE REGRESSED PATIENT. (Melitta Sperling Memorial Lecture.) L. Bryce Boyer, M.D.

Dr. Boyer discussed his experience with the psychoanalytic treatment of the regressed patient. Regarding the term "regressed patient," he acknowledged a lack of diagnostic clarity: the patients he was considering appear to range from borderline to overtly psychotic. His main thesis was that the major obstacle in the treatment of these patients is the countertransference evoked in the analyst, but that these reactions can be turned to therapeutic advantage. Dr. Boyer gave a brief historical survey of countertransference, seen as both a facilitator and inhibitor of analytic work. Freud introduced the term and considered it to be the repetition of the analyst's previously acquired irrational attitudes now directed toward the patient. It was assumed to result from the analyst's being inadequately analyzed. Fanny Hann-Kende in 1936 was the first to suggest that the analyst's reactions could be used to advantage in psychoanalytic treatment. Many authors, including Melitta Sperling, have pointed out the importance to the therapeutic process of the patient's perceptions of emotional reactions in the analyst. She wrote specifically about the psychosomatic patient in whom perception of anxiety in the analyst could lead to an exacerbation of symptoms which, she believed, were intended to elicit love from the analyst, viewed as a mother surrogate. But the exacerbation of symptoms might then be used by the anxious analyst as a reason to stop analysis, thus abandoning the patient.

The regressed patient's major mechanisms of defense were discussed next by Dr. Boyer. He presented Kernberg's concept of splitting in borderline patients: loving, fantasized relationships and hating ones are activated in the transference, but they must be split to avoid the overwhelming anxiety that would ensue if the corresponding affects of love and hate were to be experienced toward the same object simultaneously. Although this mechanism is not agreed upon by all authors as the fundamental one in the borderline patient, Dr. Boyer pointed out that all could agree on the inability of these patients to integrate and modify their impulses and affects. This problem results in the patient's experiencing the analyst as alternately omniscient and helpless, with a shift from total need for, to total devaluation of, the analyst. When the therapist needs the patient's approval for his own feeling of well-being, these shifts are particularly difficult to tolerate, and the anxiety thus provoked in the analyst often leads to countertransference reactions. The other major defense mechanism is projective identification, which involves the projection onto the analyst of repudiated aspects of the patient's personality, resulting in an identification with the analyst on the basis of these self elements. The patient then acts toward the analyst in such a way as to evoke feelings or actions that conform to the projection. If the analyst accepts the projection consciously and reacts as if the projection were a part of himself, countertransference problems are bound to occur.

[[RunningHead]]

Termination in Psychoanalysis

By Stephen K. Firestein, M.D. New York: International Universities Press, Inc., 1978. 262 pp.

Stanley Weiss

Stanley Weiss

Stanley S. Weiss
DENVER

Stanley Weiss  

This work is a textbook on termination issues based on the analyses of eight adults, four men and four women. The patients were chosen when they had reached a point at which it was likely that their treatment would be terminated within approximately two years. The clinical material was therefore followed closely by Firestein, and the clearly presented summaries of the patients' analyses do come alive. There is also a review of the literature on termination and chapters on methodological and substantive conclusions.

The analyses were conducted by candidates under supervision at The New York Psychoanalytic Treatment Center. Firestein reviewed the clinic records and interviewed the analysts, the supervisors, and the patients. The research that resulted in this book is noteworthy and timely and shows that in-depth clinical research can still be done; confidentiality can be respected and the narcissistic investment most analysts have in their work need not be an overwhelming obstacle. It is clear that analysts, in order to advance the science and teaching of psychoanalysis, are willing to share with others their understanding of theory and technique, their ways of working, and the evaluation of their results. The author received excellent cooperation from all the candidates, supervisors, clinic staff, and the patients themselves.

Firestein came to the fairly obvious conclusion that termination is an important phase of the analytic process, that it brings to the fore intense affects, and that it involves a crucial reworking of important conflicts and problems leading to personality reintegration and reorganization. He also notes that this phase does not conclude on the ending date but may persist thereafter for varying periods. Although most analysts would fully agree with this, it may need repeated rediscovery and documentation, because not very long ago in the history of psychoanalytic education many analysts felt that termination took place only when the analysis ran out of material; in other words, it was taught that termination was at hand when the analytic data "dried up.

[[RunningHead]]

Adolescent Psychiatry: Developmental and Clinical Studies. V, 1977

The Significance of the Therapist's Feelings in the Treatment of Anorexia Nervosa. Bertram J. Cohler. Pp. 352-384.

Because of the life-threatening nature of anorexia nervosa (which makes it unlike most psychiatric conditions) as well as the intense need in anorectic patients to recreate with their therapists the symbiosis with mother which is at the core of their illness, psychotherapy with these patients leads to very powerful countertransference reactions in the therapist. The author contends that, to help the patient truly resolve the original symbiosis, it is crucially important that the therapist understand and tolerate these most painful, uncomfortable emotions within her/himself for a period of time in treatment. He illustrates his thesis with a detailed case history of an adolescent girl treated for anorexia nervosa at a residential treatment center. The case clearly shows this illness to be "a symbolic expression of a patient's desperate need to maintain control … a defense against feelings of being annihilated and destroyed." The author believes that resolution of the symbiosis in the transference, not manipulation by behavior modification to control symptoms, provides cure of the illness.

[[RunningHead]]

Kohut: A Book Review Essay11

Because it emerged slowly out of evolving theory and practice, Kohut's work is much harder to bring into focus than revisions based on a concise doctrine, or a simple model, or a special animus. Ornstein (in Kohut, 1978) offers a useful guide, but of course he views the system from within the system, where empathy is already given such a singular position that it can by itself account for the development of the theory. The outside critic will have to first cast the organically developing theory into a form that feels like a progressively developing argument before he can place it in the field of contesting theories.

Lawrence Friedman M.D.

Lawrence Friedman

Lawrence Friedman, M.D.
50 East 72 Street
New York, N.Y. 10021

Lawrence Friedman  

ABSTRACT

Kohut's homeostatic account of mental events in terms of their self-preservative function may be a compromise between a theory of affective markers of psychic differentiation and a theory of self-esteem drives. Similarly, an appreciative style of treatment, designed to keep the analyst available for the exercise of growth needs, is supplemented by the interpretive task of integrating incongruent tendencies. Kohut's work raises interesting questions about theoretical circularity, freedom from a single set of conceptual principles, the value of en bloc histories of affective constellations, and the consequences of a treatment at once exculpatory and judgmental.

[[RunningHead]]

Mind and Madness in Ancient Greece. The Classical Roots of Modern Psychiatry

By Bennett Simon, M.D. Ithaca, N.Y.: Cornell University Press, 1978. 336 pp.

James McLaughlin

James McLaughlin

James T. McLaughlin
PITTSBURGH

James McLaughlin  

For those of us who share Santayana's conviction that we are doomed

312

to repeat the history we do not remember, this complex and wide-ranging work offers rich vistas of the past and the hope of enlarged perspectives on perennial problems in our field.

Bennett Simon's scholarship and insights in his "two passions—the Greek classics and—psychiatry and psychoanalysis," amply evident over some three hundred pages of heavily annotated text, make him both fine guide and good companion in this time-shuttle between the then and now of some twenty-five hundred years of human beings' efforts to know themselves in their world.

His intent is to throw light from the past on our current muddle over what is mental illness, what is treatment, what is a psychiatrist. His mode is to inform us with rich samplings of ancient and classical Greek thought and tradition regarding mind and character, madness and illness, healing and being. His strategy is to move back and forth between the current scene and the old, mirroring one with the other in amplification of both.

Thus, he schematizes the present-day babel of tongues in human psychology as a polarization between the intrapsychic (psychoanalytic) model and the social-psychiatric, with another polarity between these two and the medical model. For ancient Greece, his sortings are into yet another three modes: the poetic (chiefly Homeric), the philosophical (mainly Platonic), and the medical (the Hippocratic corpus). Here, too, he identifies significant tensions and differences in Greek thought about the value and nature of the poet, the philosopher, and the physician; the divergences and polarities of their viewpoints on the orderings of the mind; and the particular role each claimed in the healing of those disorders each sought to name.

His style is polished and coherent, but while he is scrupulous in annotating his sources and the contributions of others, his assertive mode and notational style are such that the reader must often check back to the chapteral notes to learn whether the author is asserting an original viewpoint or restating one he shares with another scholar. For this reader, the challenge added to the sense of dialogue with the author.

[[RunningHead]]

Bulletin of the Menninger Clinic. XLI, 1977

Anorexia Nervosa: An Overview. Jack L. Ross. Pp. 418-436.

Since the 1870's when Gull and Lasègue described a condition occurring primarily in pubertal girls, there has been little variation in the symptomatology of the condition presented in the literature. The syndrome is characterized by severe emaciation, amenorrhea, constipation, loss of appetite, slowed pulse and respiration, absence of somatic pathology, and strikingly contradictory need for body movement in the face of such severe wasting. Some have found Freud's assumption that impairment in the nutritional instinct was related to the organism's failure to master sexual excitation to be too narrow. Bruch, who deemphasizes intrapsychic conflict, classifies psychological weight loss into 1) psychogenic malnutrition, 2) atypical anorexia nervosa, and 3) primary anorexia nervosa, the last involving disturbances in ego functioning in the areas of body image and perception and a paralyzing sense of ineffectiveness. Psychoanalytic explanations have focused on rejection of pregnancy fantasies with regression to fantasies of oral impregnation. Many therapeutic approaches have been tried, including family therapy, behavior modification, psychotropic drugs, and psychoanalysis. Thomä, a prominent advocate of psychoanalytic psychotherapy for the condition, pointed out that the organic therapies of anorexia have been useful only in the alleviation of the acute symptoms of starvation. He has concluded that those cases receiving psychotherapy had the best prospects for recovery and that success was directly related to the patient's age at the time psychotherapy was instituted. In general, efforts to clarify the mysteries of anorexia nervosa have included biological, sociological, behavioral, and psychoanalytic approaches.

335

Bulletin of the Menninger Clinic. XLI, 1977

The So-Called Anorexia Nervosa: Diagnostic and Treatment Considerations. Charles Chediak. Pp. 453-474.

Chediak focuses on the delusional relationship between the patient and her body in describing the symptom complex of anorexia nervosa. The rapprochement crisis with its struggle surrounding separation-individuation could lead to the psychopathology of anorexia nervosa. Failure to resolve conflicts over control of the symbiotic mother leads patients to try to control all human needs by controlling hunger. In the treatment of anorexia nervosa it is fundamental to recognize the regressive re-enactment of the separation-individuation crisis during adolescence, with the patient's fear and sense of helplessness vis-à-vis the intensity of the drives. Wishes for fusion with the mother promote distortions of body image and fear of self-dissolution. The physiological dysfunctions are unavoidable consequences of the primary psychological disorder.

336

Bulletin of the Menninger Clinic. XLI, 1977

The Role of Maternal Identification in Four Cases of Anorexia Nervosa. Martin Caesar. Pp. 475-486.

S. Seides

S. Seides

S. Seides  

The author discusses four cases in which the patient's mother's wasting away from cancer seemed to be the precipitating episode in the onset of anorexia nervosa. The actual loss of the maternal object suggests the significant role of maternal identification in the psychodynamics of these cases. A repudiation of pregnancy wishes and a flight from feminine identification with regression to primitive oral mechanisms were apparent in all four cases. The relentless pursuit of thinness is in itself a maternal identification with the anorectic mother. Their denial of weight loss allows the patients to continue the aggressive assault on their bodies in order to lessen their guilt over murderous impulses.

336

Bulletin of the Menninger Clinic. XLII, 1978

The Self-Soothing Function: Its Appearance in Dreams. James L. Nash and Jesse O. Cavenar. Pp. 119-132.

Successfully analyzed patients seem to develop a self-soothing function which is heir to the therapeutic alliance between analyst and analysand. Analysis of the fundamentally narcissistic pleasure in the analytic situation itself leads to the transition from an analyst-soothing to a self-soothing function. This is attainable as a result of the earlier development of object constancy and self-cohesiveness following the rapprochement subphase and leads to the patient's ability to avoid postanalytic depression. Failure to attain an adequate self-soothing function can be traced to disturbed dyadic pregenital relationships. Thus failure to analyze the actual dyadic gratification and attachment in the analytic situation may block the transition to a self-soothing function.

336

Bulletin of the Menninger Clinic. XLII, 1978

Freud's Mysticism and Its Psychodynamic Determinants. Edwin R. Wallace, IV. Pp. 203-222.

In examining Freud's mysticism Wallace relates the superstitious elements and unusual experiences in Freud's personal life, his evaluaitons of the occult, and some of his speculative writings to his conflict with his father. Freud explained most superstitions as based on projected thoughts, fears, and wishes. He himself had a preoccupation with his own death. This was part of a fatalistic current that allowed him to project aggression against his father onto others (i.e., Breuer, Fliess, Jung). In these estrangements there occurred a repetitive acting out of the ambivalence and death wishes toward his father. Wallace relates Freud's ideas on telepathy, the supernatural, the primal father, the "double," and fantasies of immortality to his inner struggle with parricidal rage and the problem of the death instinct. Rather than experience the full measure of his ambivalence, Freud projected it into his writings on parapsychology, and it became their primary determinant.

337

Bulletin of the Menninger Clinic. XLII, 1978

Karl Menninger—Still Ahead of His Time. Lewis L. Robbins and Melvin Herman. Pp. 291-306.

In a tribute to Dr. Karl on his eighty-fifth birthday the authors write about his character traits and about the salient events of his impressively productive life to date. Included are his early interest in mental health during medical school, the encouragement he received from his close relationship with his educator-physician father in establishing jointly the Menninger Foundation, the development of his independent lines of thought, and his wide-ranging interests in child care, psychoanalysis, conservation, education, and administration. His major writings over the years are briefly mentioned as are his still active current interests.

Psychoanalytic Study of the Child. XXXII, 1977

Comments on Penis Envy and Orgasm in Women. K. R. Eissler. Pp. 29-83.

Buried in the middle of this paper is a statement that most aptly presents the challenge it undertakes: "The difficulty in finding an even half-way satisfactory theory of female sexual development is based on the plurality of factors that are relevant." These factors are discussed in detail. For example, concepts of penis envy and vaginal orgasm are the focus in Eissler's attempt to examine the current feminist challenge to classical analytic thinking on women. The effects of penis envy may vary widely with changing history. Eissler compares penis envy with sibling rivalry in its potential impact. The difficult question is not its existence, but the nature of the adult consequences of childhood penis envy. One of the many concepts critically evaluated is vaginal orgasm. Without denying Kinsey's and Masters and Johnson's evidence that no physiologic difference between clitoral and vaginal orgasm exists, he presents clinical material to support the view that psychological differences do exist, and "that women have the ability to experience orgasm in two different areas of their genital apparatus." Suggesting that physiologically identical processes may be experientially different, he proposes that the vaginal component may not reach conscious experience in all women.

In the paper's final section, Eissler will most certainly outrage what few feminists he has not yet already alienated, with his arguments supporting male superiority.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Psychoanalytic Study of the Child. XXXII, 1977

Either-Or Dilemmas. Anton O. Kris. Pp. 91-117.

Either-or dilemmas are described as conflicts, characteristically consciously experienced or brought unaltered to consciousness, that are felt by the patient to be insoluble. Invariably associated with intra- and intersystemic conflicts, they are common and pose significant therapeutic difficulties. The usual forms are active genital versus passive libidinal wishes; homosexual versus heterosexual wishes; independence versus dependence; affectionate versus sensual current. Condensation is the mechanism that most often prevents effective free association, with expression of the conflict. The conflict then remains inaccessible to the integrative functions of the ego. Mutual frustration of the paired conflictual wishes describes the dilemma. The dangers and anxieties of each side may be very different. When the conflictual wishes are bound together by obligatory condensation and inaccessible to the integrative function of the ego, efforts to satisfy the wishes of one side without arousing anxiety may bring wishes of the other side into anxiety-arousing status. The most common pair is active genital versus passive libidinal. Kris candidly states his greater confidence in his formulation than in his understanding of the origins of these dilemmas. He finds that all of his patients categorized as psychotic, borderline, or with severe narcissistic pathology demonstrate either-or dilemmas. He proposes that either-or is the inevitable and usual mode of thought until superego development is established. Although preoedipal children can make subtle cognitive differentiations, he does not believe they can sustain them under emotional pressure.

339

American Imago. XXXV, 1978

Hugo von Hofmannsthal: "Letter of Lord Chandos"—The Writer's Relationship to His Language. Judith M. Brett. Pp. 238-258.

At the age of seventeen Hofmannsthal stunned the Viennese intelligentsia with his poetry, drama, and criticism. At twenty-five he stopped writing; when he resumed three years later, he wrote in forms far different from those which had won him early fame. The three-year silence was broken by The Letter of Lord Chandos in which a fictitious young nobleman writes to Sir Francis Bacon replying to inquiries about his two years of literary silence. Brett's persuasive analysis of the Letter indicates that during Hofmannsthal's early period of creativity his relationship to language was one of symbiotic merger; after the silent period his relationship to language reflected separateness from the mother and identification with the father.

Joseph Slap

Joseph Slap  

Salinas finds that the imagery in Emerson's essay on Nature expresses fantasies of oral relatedness to the mother. The anxiety which might accompany regression to fantasies of merger and engulfment is defended against by the emphasis on "I," an active approach to the subject, and the use of the intellect. The combination of a return to the original at-one-ness with the nurturing mother along with successful defenses against the attendant dangers imparts a sense of security to this and other works by Emerson.

Cross-cultural differences in drinking habits and in alcohol-related deaths are examined in an effort to account for the unusually high incidence of alcohol poisoning in Finland. Israel Annals of Psychiatry and Related Disciplines. XVI, 1978

Three Types of Groups. J. O. Wisdom. Pp. 103-123.

It is a fundamental problem of groups that they can display behavior different from the behavior of members in isolation. Freud's theory explains this phenomenon beautifully, but his explanation turns out to apply only to a restricted type of group—one consisting in the simple summation of all the members composing it. The problem of heterogeneous groups therefore remains. Bion's theory goes a long way toward mapping the behavior of such groups; his theory may be seen as a general one embodying Freud's as a special case when the members have a common need and focus and a special kind of leader. In addition there is the problem of normality, which for Bion is achieved in the work-group. A brief indication of the relationships of these three types of groups to one another is made. The author does not attempt to provide a theory to explain group bonding.

343

Israel Annals of Psychiatry and Related Disciplines. XVI, 1978

Interminable Mourning as a Family Process. D. R. Aleksandrowicz. Pp. 161-169.

The author describes the effects of mourning on family relationships. Mourning is a normal reaction to loss, and its function is to restore the ability to love, which was impaired by the trauma of loss. In deviant, interminable mourning, the bereaved is unable to relinquish the lost object, and the capacity to love others is not restored. Under favorable circumstances, a bereaved family can shift the roles and relationships to compensate for the loss. Sharing of grief and pain can then lead to the strengthening of family ties. In cases of interminable, deviant mourning a split and a deterioration occur in the bereaved family. The author describes two families illustrating interminable mourning and split. In the first family the mother, after the death in war of her oldest son, became depressed, withdrew emotionally, and imposed a regime of permanent mourning in the home. Two of the children and the father resigned themselves to the situation and found substitute interests, but the youngest daughter rebelled and finally attempted suicide. Family counseling failed because of resistance but the threat of possible suicide by the daughter forced the mother to become reinvolved in the family. In the second family the father became seriously disturbed after the death of his teenage daughter. Family counseling was ineffective, but the patient was able to use supportive therapy to work through his feelings of loss, to overcome his reluctance to face ambivalence, and to recognize the split he had caused in the family. Interminable mourning splits off the mourner, who clings rigidly to the deceased, from the rest of the family. The mourner monopolizes the grief, and interferes with its expression by the other members of the family. The split, in the author's experiences, can be traced to previous latent tensions in the family. It is often difficult to work with a split family, and individual therapy with the mourner may be more effective.

344

Attitudes Towards Self-Poisoning among British and Israeli Doctors and Nurses in a Psychiatric Hospital. Sh. Ramon and C. E. Breyter. Pp. 206-218.

All members of the day-shift staffs in a British hospital and in an Israeli hospital (twenty-nine psychiatrists and fifty nurses) were interviewed in a replication study on attitudes toward self-poisoning patients. Although the two staffs differed in their suggestions of general reasons for self-poisoning, the motives ascribed to specific hypothetical cases and the degree of readiness to help and sympathize

345

were rather similar. Motives of "escape" and "communication" were suggested most frequently; only in one case was self-poisoning perceived as an attempt to manipulate others. Psychiatrists and nurses differed more within the British group than in the Israeli one. In both groups, however, nurses tend to be less accepting, less sympathetic, and less ready to help than doctors. The findings are discussed in relation to those obtained in the original study of staff in a general hospital.

Oedipus in the Labyrinth: A Psychoanalytic Reading of Robbe-Grillet's "In the Labyrinth." Robert Storey. Pp. 4-16.

Despite Robbe-Grillet's professions of personal concerns with style rather than content, In the Labyrinth examined analytically reveals conflicts of oedipal romance and guilt defended obsessionally. Literature and Psychology. XXVIII, 1978

Ambivalence and Identification: Freud on Literature. Françoise L. Simon-Miller. Pp. 23-40.

Freud's characterologic ambivalence, manifest in his personal life and in the dualism of his theories, was reflected in his divided attitude toward artists as both discoverers and rivals. The root lay in his childhood attitude toward his older nephew, John, who "got there first" to both woman's love and psychological truths. Since dream theory and poetic devices are parallel, dream analysis reveals in the unconscious the structure of language. The Schreber case provides an instance of Freud's linguistic approach, showing all the principal forms of paranoia to be generated linguistically. Freud's literary approach followed three stages. In the first, exemplified by his examination of Jensen's Gradiva, the text is taken to confirm clinical hypotheses. In the second, as in "The Theme of the Three Caskets," complex examination of the text with extraliterary comparisons provides a more sophisticated methodology. In the third phase, from 1919 to 1938, Freud shows a general disinterest in the study of fiction. In the essay on Dostoevsky, he returned to a clinical approach, perhaps even hostile because of the similarity of his own feelings to Dostoevsky's identification with and ambivalence toward the father. These three major examples are reviewed in detail.

346

Journal of Youth and Adolescence. VII, 1978

Current Contradictions in Adolescent Theory. John C. Coleman. Pp. 1-11.

This article points out two contradictions in current adolescent theory. The first is between the "classical" point of view, espousing the notion of "storm and stress," and the "empirical" view, supporting a concept of adolescence as relatively peaceful and harmonious. The latter approach, however, creates a second contradiction because it does not explain how young people cope with the major adaptations demanded as a result of changes in their physical, social, and emotional spheres of life. The article examines the status of concepts such as the "generation gap" and "identity crisis" and concludes with the formulation of a "focal" theory of adolescence which attempts to resolve the contradictions discussed earlier.

Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XXXIX, 1975

The Desertion of Captain Rimbaud. Alain de Mijolla. Pp. 427-458.

This article continues the theme of the enigmatic aspects of unconscious identification. The author reviews certain puzzling aspects of Rimbaud's poetic career and his complete desertion of literature at the age of twenty. De Mijolla links

170

this desertion to Rimbaud's unconscious identification with his father. He reviews the available biographical material on the elder Rimbaud, whose military career kept him, or was used to keep him, on long absences from the Rimbaud household. De Mijolla links Rimbaud's flight from literature and from his mother's influence to an effort to repeat the father's behavior. The elder Rimbaud died in 1878, a turning point in Arthur's life. The former poet then made a complete break with his mother's household and began an enactment of his father's career. Many of the geographical, linguistic, and military repetitions which de Mijolla has uncovered are quite striking. There has been a curious silence about Rimbaud's father, beginning with the family but unfortunately maintained by subsequent biographers. De Mijolla suggests that there was probably a devaluation of the father in the family and a consequent inability on Arthur's part to "father" his own works and to cope with the oedipal conflict. These conflicts led him ultimately to reject his own work as disgusting and worthless and to embark on his unconscious fantasy quest for his father.

171

The Psychoanalytic Study of Society. VII, 1976

Benin and Thebes: Elementary Forms of Civilization. Peter P. Ekeh. Pp. 65-94.

An analogy is drawn between the city-states of Benin, which flourished in Africa between the tenth and the twentieth centuries, and Thebes, the ancient Greek city where the mythical drama of Oedipus took place. In the orally transmitted folklore history of Benin there appears to be a strong theme of father-son rivalry for the royal throne, which is an essential element in the Oedipus myth regarding the ruling of Thebes. The author discusses Fromm's contention that the essence of the Oedipus myth and complex is father-son rivalry, rather than incestuous desire for the mother. He concludes that there is a need to differentiate between the Oedipus myth and the oedipus complex. The former, with its emphasis on the struggle for power within the framework of a society, is more relevant for understanding sociopolitical evolution; the latter is evidence of the emergence of the individual as an autonomous entity, differentiated from society.

The Psychoanalytic Study of Society. VII, 1976

The Life History and Creative Psychopathology of the Shaman: Ethnopsychoanalytic Perspective. Charles Ducey. Pp. 173-230.

This article is replete with dramatic data regarding shamanistic development and activity in the Siberian aboriginal culture. The author hypothesizes that the

179

shaman's early development is characterized by conditions of severe maternal deprivation, leading to intense unresolved conflicts of an oral-sadistic nature with a capacity for catastrophic regressions. During puberty and early adolescence, schizoid and hysterical symptoms develop in these children. Some of them remain mentally ill all their lives, but a few succeed in going through a terrifying regression out of which they may emerge as shaman. This regressive initiation is an actual repetition and mastery of the early trauma, with symbolic representations of the archaic part-object representations and phallic cannibalistic mother images. Through an intricate process of incorporations, introjection, identification, and, finally, mastery of the dangerous part-objects, including the fantasy of total annihilation of one's body and its subsequent restoration, the future shaman acquires the power over the "bad spirits" of damage and illness. He emerges triumphant from the battle for his own mental balance and provides a crucial element for sustenance of the mental health of the community.

The Psychoanalytic Study of Society. VII, 1976

On the Origin of Judaism: A Psychoanalytic Approach. Eric Lustig. Pp. 359-367.

The author emphasizes the many indications in the Old Testament that child sacrifice was prevalent during the primordial days of Judaism. These indications stand in contradiction to the almost exclusive weight Freud attributes to the phenomenon of parricide in Moses and Monotheism and Totem and Taboo. One can surmise that many of the Judaic ritual laws were not the result of guilt feelings for the primal crime of parricide; rather they are stern reminders of the fact that infanticide can be invoked against rebellious sons. The Passover rituals in particular are filled with remnants of the first-born sacrifice tradition. The rituals of circumcision and Pidyon Hoben (buying back the firstborn from the Cohen) are viewed as substitutes for infanticide. The author concludes with two questions. Is the emphasis on parricide in current psychoanalytic theory justified? Since the fears of children have been ascribed to castration anxiety, can it be that castration anxiety should be renamed infanticide anxiety?

181

Zellermayer discusses the incomplete formation of the function of responsibility at the conclusion of adolescence. The intentional aspect of responsibility, the theoretical dilemma between this constituent of responsibility and scientific determinism, the nature of human action and its essential relation to psychotemporal elements are considered. The role of psychotemporality, its genetic and structural aspects, its relation to guilt and self-regard and to active mastery are discussed and related to ego and self-autonomy, which provide the psychic matrix out of which responsible action can emerge.

Mother-Child Symbiotic Relationship as Represented in Different Phases of Development. D. Shreibaum and B. Gaoni. Pp. 196-205.

In this article the problem of the symbiotic relationship between mother and child is discussed. With case illustrations, the authors attempt to demonstrate the special quality of the symbiotic relationship when the process of separation-individuation is arrested. They suggest that the ambivalent quality of the bond is expressed in oversensitivity, anxiety, exaggerated worry, and mutual emotional penetration between the mother and the child. In many instances there were no early symptoms indicating this lack of separation-individuation. They became manifest only at a later stage during psychotic breakdown.

Journal of Youth and Adolescence. VII, 1978

A Shift in Emphasis: Adolescent Psychotherapy and the Psychology of the Self. Arnold Goldberg. Pp. 119-132.

The methodology of both psychoanalysis and psychotherapy, which is that of introspection and empathy, is simply not the same as that of chemistry and physics. As therapists, we are part of the system, and we cannot observe without participation. Although this is a fact of which we are all quite aware, usually we treat it as an unfortunate contaminant, and this then leads us to try to ignore its theoretical import. Classical psychoanalysis would do away with or minimize it by interpretation; the viewpoint of Kohut would replace it by transmuting internalizations as well as interpretations; but in psychotherapy we have an added task of assessing just how much we must work on the need for the elimination of the functional role of the therapist. To be sure, one must differentiate and clarify the so-called transference reactions related to the incestuous objects of childhood from those directed to self objects. This is an easier job in analysis, where the focus of the neurosis is enhanced and encouraged. In therapy, such clarity is often lacking. The psychology of the self best allows us to determine how and when we are utilized by our patients and to test how well they can handle our absence. The major advantage given to us by this perspective is that of being aware of the mirroring and idealizing aspects of self development.

American Imago. XXXV, 1978

Remarks on an Aspect of Creativity. K. R. Eissler. Pp. 59-76.

Eissler considers the creative process in genius to be psychopathological and related to paranoid schizophrenia in the sense that the creative product is a new reality which he compares to a delusion. It further resembles paranoid schizophrenia in that the ego is confronted with an overwhelming conflict between repressed and forbidden strivings and the superego. The difference lies in how the preconscious wish is handled. Commonly it leads to the formation of a delusion or the taking of some action, or a topical regression takes place leading to a dream hallucination. In the creative act a further possibility, which partakes to some extent of the other three, is realized: symbolic action which combines a near hallucinatory vision of an artistic goal, a near delusional feeling of reality toward the created content, and access to the motor system since the created work has a perceptible form.

Discussion of Dr. Richard Marohn's Chapter: A Critique of Kohut's Theory of Narcissism. Peter L. Giovacchini. Pp. 213-235.

A brief and gentle critique of Marohn's chapter leads into a lengthier, rather stern criticism of Kohut's theoretical formulations and clinical approach. Mainly, the author feels that Kohut has restated in unnecessarily new terminology important old theoretical concepts long recognized by Freud and others. Regarding treatment, Giovacchini objects to what he views as Kohut's advocacy of certain deviations from classical analytic technique (e.g., responding positively to the demands of the narcissistic patient for attention and admiration, i.e., "mirroring").
