Adolescent Psychiatry: Developmental and Clinical Studies. V, 1977

Anorexia Nervosa. Hilde Bruch. Pp. 293-303.

This is a clear review of the history of anorexia nervosa and current views about diagnosis and treatment. Bruch focuses on "primary anorexia nervosa," in which one consistently finds: 1) severe disturbance in body image; 2) confused perception and interpretation of stimuli (e.g., hunger) arising from within the body; and 3) a profound sense of ineffectiveness. Therapy must include both a restitution of normal nutrition and, in the author's opinion, psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapy geared toward helping the patient recognize and better deal with impulses, feelings, and inner needs.

The Human Mind Revisited. Essays in Honor of Karl A. Menninger

Edited by Sydney Smith, Ph.D. New York: International Universities Press, Inc., 1978. 503 pp.

Wayne Myers

Wayne Myers

Wayne A. Myers
NEW YORK

Wayne Myers  

This volume, containing nineteen essays in honor of Karl A. Menninger, begins with a brief biography, "Introduction: A Renaissance Man of Psychiatry," by Sydney Smith. In it, the influence of Dr. Karl's parents, his teacher Southard, and his analyst Franz Alexander are delineated, as is the meteoric success which followed the publication of his first book, The Human Mind.

Herbert J. Schlesinger's interesting clinical article, "Developmental and Regressive Aspects of the Making and Breaking of Promises," traces the progression from what he refers to as the stage of primary promising, in which the act of promising is regarded by the child as complete in itself, to the mature achievement of secondary promising, in which the promise is a prelude to a later act of fulfillment. He sees children's promises as "propitiary tales" couched in the future tense but intended to correct past misdemeanors and to assuage the resulting alienation from the parents.

Robert R. Holt's contribution, "Ideological and Thematic Conflicts in the Structure of Freud's Thought," continues the author's studies of Freud's cognitive style. Holt describes a series of intellectual and ideological conflicts in Freud's work, which he traces back to the influence of the conflicting cultural and scientific trends of the nineteenth century. Holt divides the contradictory doctrines and disciplines he enumerates into a "soft" side concerned with speculative and intrapsychic matters and a "hard" one imbued with the inductive reasoning of the exact sciences.

Holt speculates that the "hard" side stood for paternal authority to Freud, whereas the "soft" side came to represent the comforting embrace of the mother. He infers from this that Freud was struggling with the construction of a stable sexual identity and goes on to hypothesize that Freud's mental makeup allowed him to delay synthesis and to tolerate contradictions, thereby enabling him to be exceptionally creative. Holt finds the resolution to the contradictions in Freud's thinking in a new scientific world view based on twentieth century systems theory.

Meaning and Discourse. A Computer Model of Psychoanalytic Speech and Cognition

By John Henry Clippinger, Jr. Baltimore and London: The Johns Hopkins University Press, 1977. 231 pp.

Allan Rosenblatt

Allan Rosenblatt

Allan D. Rosenblatt
LA JOLLA, CALIF.

Allan Rosenblatt  

"How do speakers arrange linguistic items … to convey and to conceal their meanings and intentions? Or, from another perspective, what inferences can we make about a speaker's cognitive (and affective) processes from an examination of the manner in which his or her discourse is constructed?" (p. xi). This question, posed by the author as the problem to be addressed in this book, is more familiar to psychoanalysts in its second form. Indeed, it is from the latter perspective that psychoanalysis functions as a method of investigation as well as a therapeutic endeavor, developing certain hypotheses about underlying cognitive and affective activities from the data of a type of discourse, i.e., free association.

In this intriguing book, however, Clippinger has attacked the problem from the opposite direction. Starting with a conceptual framework of information processing, he has developed certain hypotheses regarding the cognitive and linguistic processes underlying discourse. He has then constructed a computer program that fairly accurately reproduces and predictably varies a selected sample of psychoanalytic disourse. The discourse episode, a patient's verbalization in a fragment of a psychoanalytic session selected from taperecorded sessions of four years of analysis, reproduces virtually every stammer, hesitation, and ungrammatical construction and clearly demonstrates the patient's uncovering, through her associations, an unconscious fantasy, as well as the interplay of associated defenses. By this successful modeling, the author has attempted to demonstrate the validity of his underlying hypotheses.

This important book attempts to demonstrate the psychological credibility of the dreams found within the extant Greek tragedies. The model for Devereux's approach is Freud's Delusions and Dreams in Jensen's Gradiva, in which Freud scrutinizes the dreams of Norbert Hanold, the fictional archeologist in search of a beautiful, elusive woman he has seen on a sculpture from antiquity. Such a study, the author argues, is meaningful only if psychoanalytic methods are applied "as if" the fictional personage's dream were that of a living person. Further, the analysis must preserve the status of the work as a work of art, that is, analysis must broaden and deepen our understanding of the text that contains a dream narrative. The book is subtitled An Ethno-Psycho-Analytical Study, for the author, a psychoanalyst as well as a distinguished anthropologist, assumes that "great art is located at the confluence of culturally imposed artistic means and objectives and a subjectively determined psychological realism" (p. xi); he is able to combine the culturally bound view of what is tragic with a more universal, psychoanalytically derived, notion of tragedy.

James Bing

James Bing

James Bing  

The authors make important observations concerning the general functioning of an analyst. The analyst's attention is divided into listening to understand and listening to communicate. Other points the authors make are: a) the necessity for the analyst's being "human," meaning not stiff and rigid but relaxed enough to show parts of his or her personality; b) that the analyst not be disconcerted by his or her own inevitable "adventitious" and "inadvertent" idiosyncracies that occur during the process of analysis. These may in fact enhance the progress of analysis. At no time do the authors imply that they should be used as ploys or contrivances.

The Annual of Psychoanalysis. V, 1977

On the Continuing Evolution of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy: Reflections and Predictions. Paul H. Ornstein and Anna Ornstein, with discussion by Abraham Zaleznik and Evelyne Schwaber. Pp. 329-370.

James Bing

James Bing

James Bing  

The authors establish a continuum from psychoanalysis and psychoanalytic psychotherapy to focal psychotherapy. They describe the therapeutic process in the psychoanalytic psychotherapies, stressing both differences and similarities. The following quotation is the gist of their main thesis: "We have placed the curative fantasy into the center of the evolving patient-therapist relationship, in order to illustrate how a narrow segment of the patient's fantasy might be activated in focal psychotherapy, a broader and deeper segment of it in psychoanalytic psychotherapy, and its most regressive and archaic roots might be activated and unfold in psychoanalysis." Thus the curative fantasy is considered to be the common denominator of these therapies.

In his discussion of the paper Zaleznik makes many interesting points, some of which are: 1) the extent to which patients differ stands in the way of attempting to unify all therapies and put them on a continuum; 2) the Ornsteins seem to leave out the important factor of resistance in establishing their theories of therapy; 3) although interpretations are important, it would have been more useful if they also had been able to address themselves to the limitations of interpretations; and 4) the fact that they insist on the concept of the continuum as described above may be a fallacious approach, but this does not minimize the remainder of their contributions. Schwaber's discussion contributes some very interesting points about empathy.

Meetings of the New York Psychoanalytic Society

January 30, 1979. A CASE OF BEREAVEMENT. Erna Furman.

Mrs. Furman's presentation marked the occasion of her receipt of the Heinz Hartmann Award of The New York Psychoanalytic Institute for her book, A Child's Parent Dies. She described three years of a boy's development, from the time of his father's death just before the boy's third birthday to the beginning of his latency period. The impact of his father's illness and death was mitigated by his mother, whom Mrs. Furman saw in weekly treatment, and by the efforts of the teaching staff of the therapeutic nursery school and kindergarten he attended from the time he was three-and-a-half years old. The therapeutic work was based on the mother's and teacher's observations, as well as on Mrs. Furman's own weekly visits at the school.

The mother had originally consulted Mrs. Furman with a prophylactic aim after the father's death. The boy, bright and very verbal, an only child of young parents, was already symptomatic. As the father became increasingly incapacitated by a depressive illness, the mother reached a decision to divorce. Upon hearing this, the father had a fit of fury and attacked the mother in front of the boy. The next day the mother found him dead, a suicide. The initial therapeutic work centered on clarifying with the child the concept of death and the events surrounding his father's death, and on helping him differentiate his own life from his father's fate.

Meetings of the New York Psychoanalytic Society

Israel Zeifman

Israel Zeifman

Israel Zeifman  

DISCUSSION: Dr. Judith Kestenberg expressed her appreciation of Mrs. Furman's study of bereavement and of her contribution to the therapeutic nursery. Addressing herself to treatment via the mother, and in the light of her own research into the developmental subphase of parenthood, she wondered about the effect on the mother's self-esteem of her realization of how she had frightened the boy with her own anger. How were the interventions modified to suit the different developmental phases he was passing through? Could his mourning and body reactions be seen as manifestations of the inner genital modality, and how can one explain the absence in the child of any reference to babies? Dr. Robert J. Kabcenell raised questions about the mother's acting as therapist and the problem of dealing with the child's aggression in a family with one surviving parent. Dr. Bernard C. Meyer inquired about creativity as a response to early parental loss, citing Saint Exupéry.

Mrs. Furman acknowledged her appreciation of Dr. Kestenberg's work and felt that the material could have been formulated in terms of the inner genital phase. She added that material from the boy about babies had been left out of the presentation. The mother was in treatment with someone during part of the time she was seeing Mrs. Furman. The words used in the treatment came from the child and in this case were filtered through the mother whose empathy smoothed the whole working process. In response to Dr. Kabcenell, Mrs. Furman reviewed her experience with mother-as-therapist, indicating that the mother-nurse and mother-teacher roles are integral to childhood.

DISCUSSION: Dr. Milton Horowitz spoke about Dr. Pfeffer's treatment of early positive experiences in which drive-attenuation or neutralization is prominent and stated that such experiences help the child to eliminate the threat of instinctual flooding in relation to primary objects. Such remembered experiences are those in which drives are tamed and from which comfort and a sense of affection can be obtained. Positive memories are organizing mental structures which have their impact upon fantasies and other memories and contribute to the development of a positive transference and working alliance.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

American Imago. XXXV, 1978

Nietzsche and the Psychology of Genius. John E. Gedo. Pp. 77-91.

Nietzsche felt that his character had been shaped by the loss of his father when he was five. He seemed to seek out and lose replacements throughout his life. Gedo speculates that his fixation to his father developed out of a sequence of events initiated by Nietzsche's slowness to talk. A physician recommended that the boy be frustrated unless he named desirable objects shown to him. Gedo reasons that the boy may have been so gravely disappointed in his previously indulgent mother that he turned decisively to his father; when the father died, the fixation became established. Nietzsche's difficulties are consistent with the prevalent belief that geniuses are necessarily significantly disturbed in their personalities. Nonetheless, Gedo has reservations about the universality of this characterization of greatness and cites Freud as a genius who was not a near-psychotic.

American Imago. XXXV, 1978

The Personality of Michelangelo Buonarroti: Some Reflections. Richard and Editha Sterba. Pp. 158-177.

Joseph Slap

Joseph Slap

Joseph Slap  

The Sterbas find that Michelangelo's personality and life course were significantly shaped by conflicts over his aggression toward his mother; she had placed him as a newborn with a wet-nurse in a stonemason's family and never took him back, dying when he was five years old. This thesis finds support in Michelangelo's renderings of the madonna who, with one notable exception, appears indifferent to the babe. In the exception, the madonna appears to be a peasant and there is a stone quarry in the background, suggesting that this madonna represents the wet-nurse. The Sterbas feel that white marble symbolized the maternal breast for Michelangelo, and they explain his savage attacks on the marble and his inhibition in beginning and completing sculptures as derivatives of these conflicts.

Adolescent Psychiatry: Developmental and Clinical Studies. V, 1977

Changing Values: Their Implications for Adolescent Development and Psychoanalytic Ideals. Aaron H. Esman. Pp. 18-34.

In this eloquently written essay the author attempts to show that the structure and expectations of the society in which we live have changed drastically from those of the society in which psychoanalysis developed. These changes (i.e., the societal questioning of all basic Judeo-Christian moral tenets) are profoundly affecting both the process of adolescence in our time and the tasks facing psychoanalysts. Esman gives evidence for his ideas that "psychoanalysis must increasingly become a psychology of development rather than merely a psychology of conflict" and that "as analysts and therapists we are concerned with repair of developmental failures rather than resolution of discrete pathogenic conflicts.

Adolescent Psychiatry: Developmental and Clinical Studies. V, 1977

On Children's Rights and Therapeutic Institutions. Derek Miller and Robert A. Burt. Pp. 39-53.

This paper offers a strong critique of proposed laws which would provide adolescents with the legal right to oppose their placement by parents or court

172

in residential facilities. The authors, a psychiatrist and a lawyer, point out the basic misunderstanding of adolescent psychology implicit in such laws: the fact that adolescents, especially disturbed adolescents, communicate far more meaningfully in actions than in words. With several clinical examples, the authors document their thesis that creating a legal adversary relationship between adolescent and helping agents is therapeutically harmful. They do suggest that courts have a positive role to play in: 1) guaranteeing right to treatment for all institutionalized adolescents; 2) scrutinizing the degree to which residential institutions interfere with personal liberty of adolescents who are not shown to present a danger to themselves and others; and 3) reserving individual hearings only for those adolescents for whom secure confinement is thought necessary.

Adolescent Psychiatry: Developmental and Clinical Studies. V, 1977

Sexuality in Adolescent Males. Judith Baskin Offer and Daniel Offer. Pp. 96-107.

The Offers have pioneered in defining criteria of normality in adolescence, and in studying in detail the attitudes and behavior of normal teenagers. Seventy-three suburban, midwestern male high school freshmen were chosen for longitudinal study on the basis of their scores on the widely tested Offer Self-Image Questionnaire. The scores were all within one standard deviation of the mean in nine out of ten scales of the questionnaire. Although this rather homogeneous group could be divided into three distinctly different groups in terms of developmental patterns, sexual attitudes and behavior could not be correlated with any other psychological variable. Within the larger groups studied by the authors, the only other variables correlated with sexual attitudes were male versus female and older adolescents versus younger ones. Delay between biological maturation and heterosexual involvement appears to be neither consistently helpful nor harmful to total psychological development. Within the small group studied, timing of sexual acts relative to age seems to reveal little about personality development of the subject.

Adolescent Psychiatry: Developmental and Clinical Studies. V, 1977

A View of Adolescent Pathology. Moses Laufer. Pp. 243-256.

This refreshingly succinct paper makes a basic point and illustrates it with clinical cases. The author strongly believes that one should clearly recognize adolescent psychopathology when it exists rather than attempting to view it as a normal part of the "youth culture." Laufer focuses on the internal life of the adolescent as the chief determinant of pathological development. He believes that adolescent pathology in various forms represents "a breakdown in the process of integrating one's physically mature body as part of the representation of oneself." Using clinical illustrations, he points out that therapeutic intervention aiding the adolescent in this task of integration is not only desirable but crucial in resolving pathological patterns which may become fixed by the end of adolescence.

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman  

By "self-disclosure" the authors apparently mean not only the sharing of personal data but also any revelation by the therapist to the patient of opinions and emotional reactions. The literature is reviewed and is thought to demonstrate that "self-disclosure per se is of little value in promoting openness by patients or in ameliorating treatment results." The authors set forth parameters to help the psychotherapist judge rationally when and when not to use self-disclosure in therapy with adolescents. They particularly caution that the therapist guard against using self-disclosures as a vehicle for acting out countertransference feelings and that it is best, before making any self-disclosures, to wait until "a clear picture of the transference-countertransference situation and the therapeutic alliance becomes discernible.

The Psychoanalytic Study of Society. VII, 1976

Janusian Thinking and Creativity. Albert Rothenberg. Pp. 1-30.

Janusian thinking—"actively conceiving two or more opposite or antithetical ideas, concepts, or images simultaneously," according to the author's definition—is proposed as a specific thought process that operates in the act of creation. The author uses the symbolic elements in Eugene O'Neill's The Iceman Cometh to illustrate the essence of simultaneous contradiction in the different structures of the play. This is supported by evidence from Oriental religions, modern music, architecture, and scientific discoveries. Janusian thinking is not solely responsible for the act of creativity, but it is a crucially important factor in diverse types of the creative process and the first specific thought process in creativity to be defined.

The Psychoanalytic Study of Society. VII, 1976

Prolonged Adolescence and Early Identification. L. Bryce Boyer and Ruth M. Boyer. Pp. 99-106.

In this concise article the authors use data of psychological testing and anthropological observation to postulate a theory regarding elements in the identification process. A community of Apache Indians was found to have among its school-age children, as well as among its elders, two distinct groups using similar modalities of thinking. The parents of the children, however, did not show evidence of that thinking modality. The explanation was found in the observation that parenting in this tribe is characterized by severe inconsistency and neglect due to abnormally prolonged adolescent behavior on the part of the parents, which lasts until about age forty. The maternal grandmothers usually step in and provide a more mature, loving, and consistent presence.

The Psychoanalytic Study of Society. VII, 1976

Ghost Sickness and Superego Development in the Kiowa Apache Male. Daniel M. A. Freeman; Edward F. Foulks; Patricia A. Freeman. Pp. 123-172.

The description of the striking phenomenon of the "ghost sickness"—a massive hysterical conversion often occurring as an element in a mourning process—is given in thorough detail. Conceptualization of the phenomenon follows the theoretical framework of the separation-individuation process as described in the previous article, particularly the aspects of superego formation emphasized there. The authors contend that ghost sickness occurs when a mourning process takes place in individuals who were unable to integrate the aggressive and idealized images of the parental introjects. At the time of mourning the aggressive elements are projected and perceived as a threatening, ominous ghost image that is trying to pull the victim toward death. Reunion wishes and oral-incorporative fears are implied in this condition as well.

The Psychoanalytic Study of Society. VII, 1976

Magic and Healing: An Ethnopsychoanalytic Examination. Richard Day and Ronald H. Davidson. Pp. 231-292.

This articles bears direct relevance to the one preceding it. It attempts to answer the question of what enables some obviously traumatized, seriously disturbed members of a sociocultural group to attain the important stabilizing identity of a shaman or faith healer, while others succumb to their unresolved conflicts and become identified as "sick." A metapsychological proposition is offered by the authors, implying the existence of an "ethnic unconscious." Those individuals who are capable of communicating their idiosyncratic primary process productions in symbols that resonate with the symbolic system of the ethnic unconscious retain their capacity to remain integrated with society. Also, their defensive structure must be "culturally sanctioned," their role corresponding with that of an artist in our society. A detailed presentation of a Philippine female faith healer comprises the bulk of the article.

The Psychoanalytic Study of Society. VII, 1976

The Subarctic Atabascans of Alaska: The Ecological Grounding of Certain Cultural Personality Characteristics. Arthur E. Hippler; L. Bryce Boyer; Ruth M. Boyer. Pp. 293-330.

The Atabascan people inhabit the harsh and barren land of subarctic Alaska. The scarcity of food forced them to spread over vast areas in small, matrilineal hunting and gathering groups. These people are distinguished by a specific "cultural personality," as defined by the authors. They are highly suspicious, even paranoid, toward all who are not members of their family and are preoccupied with dread, imaginary monsters which populate their environment. Suggestible, gullible, impulsive, and subject to hysterical illnesses, they lack tenderness in sexual relationships, and the attitudes of parents toward their young is extremely ambivalent. They seem to be able to lose loved ones without evidence of pain or suffering and in general to exhibit stoic attitudes and suppress any intense emotions.

The Psychoanalytic Study of Society. VII, 1976

The Mackenzie Delta Eskimos: Problems of Adaptation to Changing Social and Economic Conditions. Joseph M. Lubart. Pp. 331-357.

Social and individual patterns established over the span of many generations of the Land Eskimos of the Mackenzie Delta became severely disrupted by the encounter with white North American civilization. For the male Eskimo, whose self-esteem depended on success as a provider in a whaling, hunting, or trapping economy, the new "welfare economy" proved to be devastating. The dwindling of food supplies (disappearance of the caribou herds) and the establishment of white Canadian outposts in the Mackenzie Delta caused the migration and centralization of the Eskimos from the vast territories to the few white dominated centers. There they are devoid of productive functions and depend almost exclusively on government funds. Under the new circumstances most of the traditional patterns of control of destructive impulses became irrelevant. Of great importance is the precarious balance that existed between males and females. For generations, women controlled their resentment of the dominant males because of their total dependency on them as food providers. With the new economic order, the females are overtly disparaging of the Eskimo males and slavishly admire the white males, by whom they are ruthlessly exploited. The males, functionless and rejected, abuse alcohol in a frenzied manner and commit suicide in almost epidemic proportions (eight times the Swedish rate).

181

The Psychoanalytic Study of Society. VII, 1976

Origins of the Passover Seder in Ritual Sacrifice. Kurt Schlesinger. Pp. 369-399.

Daniel Birger

Daniel Birger

Daniel Birger  

Schlesinger proposes that a cyclical ceremonial rite of passage involving human and totemic animal sacrifices became condensed with other communal activities and that these lost their archaic qualities through modifications and became

181

symbolic representations of new ideological and ethical concepts. Despite heavy historical layers superimposed on them, it is possible to discern their origins and their vicissitudes. The author carefully analyzes the current practice of the Seder ritual to detect traces of Dionysian rites and ceremonials that often included human sacrifice. He supports the theory that early monotheism was the result of condensation of two sects of priests, the Kohanim and the Quadeshim, with the Kohanim gaining the upper hand after a prolonged struggle. The Quadesh priests worshipped a female deity whose temple was a center of ritualized prostitution. The Hebrew language contains a root word, Kadesh, which carries the meaning of both "holy" and "harlot," seemingly a remnant of that struggle. A discussion of ritual human sacrifice leads to the conclusion that it constitutes a breakthrough of primary process fantasies leading to an altered state of consciousness during which the fantasies are acted out. The fact that these breakthrough phenomena are harnessed by group ceremonial activity contributes to ego mastery, forges communal bonds, and solidifies the group's rules. Multiple indications of ritualized sacrifice of the firstborn son, modified and molded into the Seder ritual, are elucidated in a detailed historical analysis of the ritual. The redemption theme of the Seder is repeated on all levels—a liberation of libidinal and aggressive drives in the form of acting out of unconscious fantasy, the freedom from fear and tyranny of the primitive drives by substituting an animal sacrifice for a human one, and finally, the redemption of the tribal liberation from the oppression in Egypt.

182

Meeting of the New York Psychoanalytic Society

May 16, 1978. EXAMINATION ANXIETY IN WOMEN. Eleanor Galenson, M.D.

Dr. Galenson noted that many of her women patients exhibited a unique clinical syndrome when faced with graduate school examinations. Their symptoms were related to fear of competing with men and seemed to include important aspects of the more general problem of female self-esteem. While quite different in character structure and psychopathology, these patients all manifested similar examination anxiety which was derivative of three major preoedipal factors: fear of object loss, fear of loss of body integrity, and fear of genital imperfection. For example, eating binges, intense feelings of emotional isolation, and retreats into sleep all reflected oral phase anxieties and fear of separation from the mother. Exaggerated concerns over body imperfections often accompanied strong feelings of intellectual inadequacy and were associated with earlier fears of shame and humiliation, linked to sadomasochistic fantasies involving excretory functions and toilet training. Fear of genital imperfection expressed in the analyses led to early childhood memories of exploratory games and deep fears of being revealed as missing something—a defect which these patients felt was the basis of their "stupidity" and intellectual "phoniness."

Acknowledging that penis envy was intimately involved in this syndrome, Dr. Galenson emphasized the striking correspondence between these reactions and the preoedipal castration reactions seen in direct observation of girls between the ages of eighteen and twenty-four months. During these months a phase of early genital masturbation was noted which was always followed by a marked reaction to the genital differences between the sexes. These reactions varied from mild anxiety, with subdued affects and an obvious sense of loss, to intense, behaviorally disruptive castration anxiety. The milder reaction occurred in children whose earlier relationship with the mother was strong, and it was usually followed by a preoedipal shifting to the father and a clear facilitation of the little girls' fantasy lives and graphic representations.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Meeting of the Psychoanalytic Association of New York

March 20, 1978. THE ANALYST'S EMOTIONAL REACTIONS TO HIS CHILD AND ADOLESCENT PATIENTS AND THEIR PARENTS. Jules Glenn, M.D. and Isidor Bernstein, M.D.

Presenting a clinical vignette concerning the treatment of a latency child and his family, the authors drew attention to the variety of personal emotional

184

reactions experienced in the course of the analytic work. These could be classified as: (1) countertransferences; (2) transferences to the patient; (3) identifications; (4) instances of experiencing the patient as an extension of the analyst's self; and (5) reactions to the patient as a real person. The last group included (a) empathic responses which can generate insight, (b) signal affects which can also be used adaptively, and (c) failures to achieve empathy.

The authors distinguished countertransference reactions from other transferences to the patient by limiting the term to unconscious transferences of the analyst emerging in response to the patient's transferences. An analyst may have transferences rigidly frozen into his or her functioning, similar to character traits, which could repetitively invade the therapeutic work. Identification with the patient is not uncommon in child analysis, often appearing as part of the analyst's transferences to the parents of the child, equated with the analyst's parents. Reactions to the patient as a real person would be illustrated by the inevitable emotional response to a patient's sudden physical assault on the analyst. Although such responses are available to consciousness, self-analysis is indicated to ferret out the tranference aspects of the reaction involved.

When countertransferences are understood, particularly through the analyst's awareness of his or her accompanying affective state, they help to identify and interpret the patient's provoking transferences. Other, less intense feelings on the part of the analyst contribute to the empathy essential to the understanding of patients and their communications. The term signal affect may be applied to the relatively faint emotions which alert analysts to the correct empathic responses and aid them in the rejection of personal identifications and projections which have little to do with patients and their productions.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Meeting of the Psychoanalytic Association of New York

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey  

DISCUSSION: Dr. Alan J. Eisnitz stressed that failure to understand the patient poses a narcissistic threat to the analyst and facilitates the establishment of countertransference reactions. Defining countertransference as the persistent mobilization in the analyst of an unconscious wish and the defenses against that wish evoked by the patients, their fantasies, or the analyst's fantasies about the patients, Dr. Eisnitz suggested that identification and treating patients as an extension of the self should be considered narcissistic transference. As a consequence of the ongoing and intense relationship with the parents of a child in analysis, unconscious reactions to the analyst's own infantile objects may more easily be stimulated. The unconscious tendency to try to prove that analysts are better parents than either their own parents, their analysts, or their child patient's parents leads to a common countertransference attitude, one that might well be a potential factor in every intense adult-child relationship. Dr. Peter B. Neubauer suggested that not all the reactions to the patient described by the authors were specific to child analysts. Adults reporting material from different developmental levels may produce the same kind of reactions in the analyst. He also noted two major differences between child and adult analysis: the absent or minimal transference neurosis in children and the necessity for immediate responses with children. Immediate action on the part of the child analyst stimulates a variety of feelings and responses in both patient and analyst. Dr. Harold P. Blum observed that child analysts often serve as an auxiliary ego for the child and the child's parents. As a consequence, they will frequently be asked to provide advice and guidance but must resist the temptation to abuse their position or their knowledge.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Literature and Psychology. XXVIII, 1978

Literary Masters and Masturbators: Sexuality, Fantasy, and Reality in Huckleberry Finn. Charles E. May. Pp. 85-92.

Warren Poland

Warren Poland

Warren Poland  

Contrary to the views of critics who find the Huck Finn center section of Twain's classic realistic and the Tom Sawyer opening and closing chapters trivial, May regards the latter as an essential frame containing the concealed latent sexuality. Twain's conflict between sexuality and purity manifests itself in Huckleberry Finn as a conflict between fantasy and reality. Twain's anally bawdy "1601" and his talk, "Some Thoughts on the Science of Onanism," are considered in terms of adolescent concerns with breaking wind and masturbation. Twain referred to "old masters" as "an abbreviation, a contraction." Masturbation involves temporary regression from outer toward inner reality, a process also central to literary creativity. The production of a work of art requires a return to work in contrast to the nonproductive play of "farting around" or "playing with yourself." Thus, though the book is a serious work of art, the Tom Sawyer fantasy frame shows it is also a form of masturbatory play that masters its own sub-universe of fable. While Huck Finn may escape civilization, Sawyer and Twain subvert it with play.

374

Dimensions of Human Potentiality. The Collected Works of Eugene Pumpian-Mindlin

Edited by Michael T. McGuire, M.D. New York/London: Spectrum Publications, Inc., 1978. 333 pp.

Max Warren

Max Warren

Max Warren
SOUTHFIELD, MICH.

Max Warren  

This chronologically presented collection of the writings of Eugene Pumpian-Mindlin is representative of the breadth and depth of his clinical and theoretical interests during his professional career. Its nineteen papers deal with many different topics, such as traumatic war neuroses, psychoanalysis as theory and science, psychosomatic medicine, short-term psychotherapy, psychotherapeutic technique, and psychoanalysis and literature. The papers are uneven in quality, yet among them are such gems as: "Omnipotentiality, Youth and Commitment" and "Comments on Techniques of Termination and Transfer in a Clinic Setting," demonstrating Pumpian-Mindlin's ability to apply psychoanalytic principles to a diverse group of interests.

The Annual of Psychoanalysis. V, 1977

The Wolf Man and the Paranoid Process. W. W. Meissner. Pp. 23-74.

James Bing

James Bing

James Bing  

The author bases his thesis for the Wolf Man's pathology and particularly for his paranoid development and his narcissistic character structure on the following: "the introjective configuration forms the critical core of internalizations around which the self-system is organized and in terms of which the sense of self takes shape." Thus the basis of the author's understanding of the Wolf Man and his pathological processes is on Kleinian and Kohutian theories combined with some of the author's own ideas in connection with introjections and projections. He contributes some fascinating ideas to the further understanding of the Wolf Man, but at the same time, in this abstractor's opinion, it is a one-sided picture.

La Doctrine De Michaël Bálint. Essai De Compréhension De L'Oeuvre De Michaël Bálint À Partir D'Une Critique De Son Histoire Et D'Une Exégèse De Ses Écrits. (The Doctrine of Michael Bálint. An Essay on Understanding the Work of Michael Bálint, Starting from a Review of his History and an Exegesis of his Writings.)

By Dr. Franck Faure. Paris: Payot, 1978. 262 pp.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson, Jr.
PRINCETON, N.J.

Emmett Wilson  

Balint once wrote that his work was "known, tolerated, perhaps even read, but certainly not quoted." Unfortunately, Balint is one of those important psychoanalytic thinkers who has remained a marginal figure, never quite influencing the mainstream of psychoanalytic theory. His untimely death in 1970 came perhaps before the completion of his research and any chance to summarize conclusions from it. Sutherland, in his obituary,1 suggested that an appraisal of Balint's work would be a major task. This study of Balint by Franck Faure, a French specialist on Balint, does much to make clear the main themes of Balint's work and the development of his theoretical position and suggests the relevance of Balint for much that has developed later in psychoanalytic theorizing.

Faure concentrates on the written works, eschewing the less accessible oral tradition of the Balint groups in existence in England and on the Continent. The study proceeds in a biographical manner, beginning with the brief, brilliant years of the "Budapest school" and the influence of Ferenczi on the development of Balint's ideas. Following Balint's flight to safety in England in 1939, when he took up residence in Manchester, a period of withdrawal or apparent unproductivity set in. Faure suggests that this period was difficult professionally, financially, personally, and psychologically. A new phase of Balint's work began with his appointment to a position in London in 1945. In 1948 he joined the staff of the Tavistock Clinic and worked there at first with the Family Discussion Bureau (1948-1953). Later he began his very significant work with general practitioners' groups (from 1953 onward).

Faure insists strongly on the unity of Balint's work and attempts to show how the later Balint of The Basic Fault2 developed out of his

1Sutherland, J. D.: Michael Balint (1896-1970). Int. J. Psa., LII, 1971, pp. 331-333.2Balint, M.: The Basic Fault. Therapeutic Aspects of Regression. London: Tavistock, 1968. Reviewed in This QUARTERLY, XXXIX, 1972, pp. 129-130.

responseSet.title: Freud's Early Psychology of the Neuroses. A Historical Perspective: By Kenneth Levin.  Pittsburgh:  University of Pittsburgh Press, 1978.  314 pp.
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Freud's Early Psychology of the Neuroses. A Historical Perspective

By Kenneth Levin. Pittsburgh: University of Pittsburgh Press, 1978. 314 pp.

Walter Stewart

Walter Stewart

Walter A. Stewart
NEW YORK

Walter Stewart  

This is a very challenging book to review. It is a scholarly book which reflects the fact that it began as a doctoral thesis. An advantageous

706

consequence of this is that the study is not restricted to a review of Freud's early papers, but also investigates the times of which they were a part. It truly offers a detailed historical perspective. For the first time Freud's ideas can be understood in relation to the then current medical and psychological views. The study presents in detail the fascinating picture of the growth of Freud's ideas as they became free of the restrictions of current formulations, and the book shows how he achieved the intellectual independence that allowed him to develop a new theory of science as well as new formulations of mental processes.

Levin's extensive knowledge of the "climate" of the scientific theory of the period allows him to challenge the current view that Freud's physiological training was the basis for his later psychological formulations. He traces the history of patho-anatomical formulations in psychiatry and details the increasing emphasis on dynamic formulations. It is clear that Freud believed that both physiological and psychological formulations were required in order to arrive at an understanding of hysterical phenomena.

When discussing such well-known subjects as Freud's theory of defense and the role of sexuality in the etiology of the neuroses, the author cites a wide range of references which give fresh meaning to the issues involved. It would take more detailed recognition of the extensive references which make the book so valuable to make a review more complete and to do justice to the volume. The only criticism is that the book, having originated as a doctoral dissertation, is written more for the eyes of a committee than as an easy communication to the reader.

The reading is demanding, but it is also rewarding. The book is excellent and fully recommended.

707

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XL, 1976

The Child Psychoanalyst and the Dream. Serge Lebovici. Pp. 11-29.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Lebovici is concerned with the systematic study of children's dreams, an area which he feels has been little studied as yet. The psychoanalysis of children permits insight into the transformation of the dream work. The disguised representation of the dream wish is of much less importance in children's dreams than it is in the dream work of the adult. In children the psychic excitation draws on memories of unsatisfied wishes, but these are not, as in the adult, repressed memories. Even in latency, when there is a greater degree of psychological development, there is still relatively little disguise of the dream in its manifest content. Nevertheless there are some theoretically interesting complexities in the dreams of children. For example, we may find that the dream may be a sort of actual neurosis which is disorganizing and traumatic in itself and may sometimes be the source of post-traumatic organization. This is frequently the case with repetitive dreams in childhood, as in the case of the Wolf Man. Continuing research on trauma and the function of anxiety would lead us, then, to attach great importance to a study of the dreams of childhood. While Piaget has studied the developing attitudes of the child toward the recitation of dreams, emphasizing the evolutive, genetic, and operational aspects of the dream, psychoanalytic studies of children's dreams are much more difficult to carry out. There are difficulties in dissociating fantasy and dream productions in the child. Drawing and games seldom lead the child to talk of dreams. Lebovici finds that in his experience there are rarely important human figures in the dream text. A technique which usually reveals the persons involved is to ask the child to draw the menacing figures in the dream. Little Hans's addition of his father's moustache to his drawing of the menacing horse aided in understanding his conflicts. Although the dream wish is little disguised in the child, the displacements of affect which dissemble the intensity and meaning of the wish are more or less those one would observe in an adult.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XL, 1976

Sleep, Dream, and Instincts: An Interdisciplinary Approach. Mauro Mancia. Pp. 31-58.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Mancia discusses the view that dreaming is an instinctual activity, a view which ethologists, neurophysiologists, and psychologists have come to advocate. Yet the picture of dreaming as instinctual behavior is incomplete, and we are dealing with a number of hypotheses on the realization of instinctual behavior during sleep. Mancia reviews the ethological and neurophysiological aspects of dreaming, as well as the data from experimental psychology and psychoanalysis. He advances the hypothesis that sleep is a particular instinctive activity in which there are alternative rhythmic appetitive and consummatory phases in regular and characteristic sequence for each individual. He links the narcissistic libido of the newborn to the REM sleep which dominates the neurophysiological functioning of the first period of growth. The sleep of the newborn represents a state of absolute narcissism, autoerotism, and omnipotence. Mancia claims that the advancing developmental process and the progressive formation of object relations bring about a progressive abandonment of this narcissistic position, parallel to a reduction in sleep in general and REM sleep in particular.

Presence and Absence of Dreams as the Signal of Anxiety. Jacques Caïn. Pp. 119-123.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Some patients cannot sleep because they fear dreaming, and some cannot sleep because they fear not dreaming. Caïn suggests that the metapsychological analysis of these phenomena should rely on Kohut's concept of the self, in which the self is a theoretical concept at a low level of theorizing. It is not a system but a mental content with representations in the ego, superego, and id. The total decathexis occurring during sleep brings about a discontinuity, but one which permits a narcissistic restoration. Dreaming brings about the maintenance and intactness of the self and of a continuum in the individual's psychic life. A patient might fear going to sleep because the anxiety-provoking content of dreams threatens the destruction of the integrity of the self. On the other hand, the absence of any memory of dreams during sleep may be experienced as an emptiness which is also frightening, a discontinuity in the experience of the self. In either case the dream is a signal of anxiety, whether it brings about the anxiety, or whether, by its presence, it diminishes anxiety.

The Dream as an Object and the Dream World. Jean Guillaumin. Pp. 125-156.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

J. B. Pontalis has proposed a view of the dream as a transitional object, oscillating between the me and the not-me, between subjectivation and objectivation. Guillaumin questions the designation of the dream as a transitional object, for a transitional object begins with something concrete, a physical object, as a necessary support for the fantasy activity involved. There is no such corporality, of course, to the dream. It would be most tenuous to designate the telling of the dream as the material reality, and even Pontalis rejects this approach. There is, nevertheless, an intuitive aptness to Pontalis's view, because the dream has a sort of metabolic value for the psychic life. Guillaumin rejects Masud Khan's attempt to substitute "dream experience" for this concept, as too lost in Winnicottian vagueness. Guillaumin offers his own term, "dream world," to emphasize these transitional and creative aspects of the dream. As for the materiality involved, it is the dreamer himself. In his search for identity, the dreamer has traversed concrete, material reality in illusory fashion.

Some Determinants of Maternal Attachment. Gail H. Peterson and Lewis E. Mahl. Pp. 1168-1173.

The authors conducted prenatal interviews and behavior observation sessions with forty-six families in which the woman was pregnant. These families were again interviewed and observed seven days, one month, two months, and six months after the child was born. The authors found that the most significant variable predicting differences in maternal attachment was the length of separation of mother and infant: less separation was associated with greater attachment. The next most significant variable was birth experience, followed in importance by the length of labor and prenatal attitudes and expectations.

Coping Styles of 34 Adolescents with Cerebral Palsy. Klaus K. Minde. Pp. 1344-1349.

The author presents a follow-up study of thirty-four children with cerebral palsy. Eight years previously twenty-three of these children were attending a special school for handicapped children, and eleven were attending regular schools. The author evaluated the children and their families through formal and informal interviews and by administering parent and teacher rating scales of the children's behavior. He found that the development of these children between the ages of ten and fourteen was highlighted by their increased awareness and their parents' awareness of the permanence of their handicap and their consequent search for personal and, ultimately, occupational identity in the face of their parents' emotional withdrawal.

Private Practice of Psychiatry: Future Roles. Zigmond M. Lebensohn. Pp. 1359-1363.

Psychiatrists in private practice have contributed more to treating the mentally ill in America than is generally known. The private practice sector may be viewed as a massive national outpatient and inpatient service for the mentally ill. The impact of national health insurance on the future character of the private practice of psychiatry and the thorny problems to be resolved are discussed and compared with the experiences of England, the Soviet Union, and China. Future trends will most likely include increased emphasis on adjuvant techniques, greater emphasis on resident training in general psychiatry, briefer forms of therapy, and psychiatry's return to the medical model.

Blind Ratings of Mother-Infant Interaction in Home Movies of Prepsychotic and Normal Infants. Henry N. Massie. Pp. 1371-1374.

Home movies of infants later diagnosed as having early childhood psychoses were compared with movies of normal control infants. A scale of attachment indicators measured mother-infant dyadic avoidance and reciprocity in the first six months of the infant's life. Three judges blind to diagnosis saw a general trend toward dampened interaction for prepsychotic infants and their mothers. Prepsychotic and normal infants were not significantly different in touching and eye gaze behaviors, whereas mothers of prepsychotic infants exhibited less adequate eye gaze and touching than mothers of normal infants.

Psychological Observations of Bank Robbery. Donald A. Johnston. Pp. 1377-1379.

Bank robbery has been only partially examined in the psychiatric literature. It has been publicly considered an act of men of strong will to obtain money. According to the author's observations in a federal penitentiary, bank robbery more often is a symptomatic act with psychological meaning. The author describes several of the unconscious motives and defensive aspects of bank robbery in the hope that this will assist in demythologizing the bank robber.

Genetic Counseling for Psychiatric Patients and Their Families. Ming T. Tsuang. Pp. 1465-1475.

The author presents an overview of genetic counseling for psychiatric patients and their families, including a brief summary of contemporary research into the evidence of genetic factors, the familial risks, and the possible modes of inheritance for major psychiatric disorders. The purpose is to review and condense the available literature pertaining to psychiatric genetic counseling for the benefit of psychiatrists and counselors in their day-to-day practice and for the general "consumer." It is hoped that giving the general public access to such information will help to reduce the suffering commonly brought about by the stigmatization of those with mental disorders.

The authors present the proposed DSM-III classification of the traditional hysterical disorders, i.e., disorders that suggest physical illness but in which psychological factors are judged to be of importance. Sempell examines the relationship between Bismarck's unconscious infantile conflicts with his older brother, in particular Bismarck's wish to be first, and his later diplomatic successes. In the course of his diplomatic maneuverings Bismarck excluded the previously dominant German-speaking state, Austria, and made Prussia, with whom he was identified, pre-eminent in the German confederation. The author views this activity as a working out in an international forum of Bismarck's unconscious conflicts. Bismarck's youthful preoccupation with gambling and his transformation of this into political gambles are viewed from the vantage point of postulated omnipotent fantasies of childhood.

Linguistic Negation in Autistic and Normal Children. Theodore Shapiro and Richard Kapit. Pp. 337-351.

Young, severely maladaptive autistic children with some speech competence were compared to normally developing three-year-old children of lower and middle class and five-year-old children of lower class on negation tasks. All subjects were shown twelve sets of cards depicting negative contrasts designed to elicit semantic categories of nonexistence, denial, and rejection, and were tested for production, imitation, and comprehension. Syntactic and semantic analysis revealed that autistic children were superior imitators and poor producers but showed skills in comprehension comparable to a four-year-old's level of functioning. While retarded in some functions, the experimental group produced syntactic structures that were more rigid, suggesting the significantly greater use of imitation as a major strategy in linguistic coding.

Journal of Youth and Adolescence. VII, 1978

Work Ethic of Gifted Black Adolescents. Fred Schab. Pp. 295-305.

The attitudes and opinions of 15 gifted Black male and 152 Black female adolescents toward their future in the world of work were surveyed. Under headings of self-determination on the job, rewards, and work philosophy, significant differences were found between the sexes. Males demanded more freedom and independence, yet would be more willing to unionize. They also believed men to

349

be the main breadwinners and marriage more important to females. Gifted males wanted to surpass the successes of their parents more than did their gifted female peers. The latter would not tolerate poor working conditions as often as would the males. Thus, among gifted Black adolescents the world of work is still the domain of the male.

DISCUSSION: Dr. Charles Sarnoff pointed out that Dr. Grolnick referred to symbols in the generic sense without differentiating subdivisions such as the psychoanalytic symbols used in art. While one level of symbol can be associated with transitional objects, this does not mean that more mature levels of symbol formation stem from the same root. Dr. Sarnoff presented evidence in support of the

353

view that the development of the symbolizing function goes through many stages from the first months of life till the age of fourteen. The transitional object is not even an organizer when seen within the context of this broader view. Dr. Sarnoff called attention to data that made some of Dr. Grolnick's conclusions about the meanings of the symbols in Etruscan art rather doubtful. Seneca's comments on the Etruscans emphasized a primitiveness and concreteness in their thinking; this points toward a level of cultural evolution at which symbol formation is limited by a cognition in which abstract thinking is not central. Thus, some of Dr. Grolnick's conclusions might be challenged by taking into account the observations of a writer who had actual contact with the Etruscans. Dr. Gilbert J. Rose suggested that Dr. Grolnick's developmental metaphor requires the corrective of a consideration of the ego to avoid being reductionistic. We are accustomed to think of regression and progression as a cyclic dissolution and reconstitution which takes place during the course of development, but both experimental and analytic data suggest that this is also a moment by moment phenomenon. A recurrent expansion and constriction of ego boundaries in relation to key ego functions or an interaction of primary and secondary processes may be seen as a "transitional process," thus putting it in relation to early development and the transitional object. As visual art forms magnify the interaction between primary and secondary perception, so literary forms magnify the fluid interaction between primary and secondary elements in thought. In the transition between them Freud postulated an initial motoric phase, then primitive ideation, dreams and images, and finally verbalized thought. In creative work there is a two-way traffic between motoric elements of the primary process and discursive meanings. Dr. Rose agreed that both a child's transitional object and an Etruscan burial symbol bridge the uncertainties inherent in life, but from the point of view of the ego, perception and thought operate contemporaneously, at the same time regressive, progressive, and integrative.

Fraiberg and her co-workers studied ego development in children with three kinds of defects: blindness, deafness, and thalidomide birth defects. With "proper" mothering, the traumata resulting from all three defects were eventually overcome. The most striking finding was that blind children show the greatest lag in ego development. Thus vision appears to be the most important biological given, without which "abnormal" ego development will occur. It must be noted that autism occurs much more frequently in blind children than in sighted children, but only when the "mothering" was inadequate.

Freud's Adolescence and the Prolegomena to Psychoanalysis. Harry Trosman. Pp. 215-222.

The adolescence of creative individuals appears retrospectively preparatory. It is a period of apprenticeship permitting ego integrations of new identifications and the amalgamation of attachments from the past with goals for the future. A period of moratorium during which there is seeming inactivity permits the consolidation of new skills and interests. In Sigmund Freud's case, the period of early adolescence (following the onset of puberty) may have provided an opportunity for psychological discoveries through experiments with free association. These insights were repressed in later adolescence and did not reach fruition until subsequent maturity of the ego had taken place. It is suggested that early adolescence permits a prepatterning for later creative activity and the nascent contents are an anlage for the subsequent creativity.

Journal of Youth and Adolescence. VII, 1978

The State of Research on Ego Identity: A Review and Appraisal. Part I. Edmund Bourne. Pp. 223-251.

Considerable research on ego identity has appeared over the past fifteen years, indicating the need for an overall review. Part I commences by considering the complexity of Erikson's concept and suggesting several different theoretical contexts in which it has been used. The validity of investigators' attempts to utilize the concept "ego identity" is assumed to depend in part upon their interpretations of its meaning. The review of empirical literature is organized according to different procedures which have been used to measure ego identity. A first section summarizes and evaluates research utilizing Q-sort and self-report questionnaire measures, while a second considers the large number of investigations that have employed James Marcia's Identity Status Interview. The latter group of studies are ordered according to the type of dependent variable (e.g., cognitive, behavioral, personality, developmental) examined in relation to ego identity status (i.e., achievement, moratorium, foreclosure, diffusion).

October 31, 1978. MODIFICATIONS IN THE CLASSICAL PSYCHOANALYTIC MODEL OF ADOLESCENCE. Peter Blos, Ph.D.

Recapitulation of earlier conflicts in adolescence is more than a revival of phallic conflicts, according to Dr. Blos. The positive oedipal conflict undergoes a resolution before the latency period sets in, but the negative component reaches a conflictual crisis during adolescence. Thus the specific task of this period is to complete—not just repeat—the resolution of the oedipus complex. Adolescents can best utilize this second chance if they have acquired the appropriate ego differentiation during latency and avoided a fixation at the level of infantile narcissism. They are then able to test reality more critically, particularly in the world of object relations, and employ the social surroundings for sublimations and identifications.

Although bisexuality is relatively well tolerated in prelatency, at puberty it leads to problems of homosexuality and sexual identity and is therefore stubbornly repressed and denied. This is often accomplished by pushing heterosexual behavior and fantasies into the center of therapy and life. In resolving the negative oedipus complex, neutralization of drive components through emotional attitudes, character traits, and sublimatory endeavors is important. However, Dr. Blos also stressed a critical intermediate step, whereby the libido invested in the narcissistic object of the negative oedipal attachment becomes desexualized and initiates the structure of the adult ego ideal. The infantile belief in the magical realization of perfection is replaced by the drive toward its approximation. Thus the adult ego ideal is the heir to the negative oedipus complex.

Development during adolescence also necessitates the recapitulation and divestiture of infantile dependencies by means of a delimited, nondefensive regression. Preoedipal conflicts are usually suggested when the adolescent manifests such symptoms as dysphoric moods, overeating, or drug use, or when the patient revives the preoedipal idealized object in the transference through an attitude of unshakeable trust in the therapist. Dr. Blos believes that the process of deidealization of object and self is a most delicate task and represents the single most distressful and tormenting aspect of this phase of growth. The transference reaction is often useful in distinguishing between the patient with developmental arrest who has intense needs and the patient who has the capacity to tolerate the frustrations and thwarted expectations of the therapeutic situation.

April 17, 1978. TRUTH FROM GENETIC ILLUSION: THE TRANSFERENCE AND THE FATE OF THE INFANTILE NEUROSIS. Joseph T. Coltrera, M.D.

Stressing that consistency and accuracy of genetic interpretation and reconstruction are essential to an effective working through process if an analysis is to enhance the synthetic and integrative functions of the ego, Dr. Coltrera raised several questions concerning the tendency to deal with the transference neurosis solely in dynamic terms. Noting Freud's distinction between interpretation and reconstruction and his emphasis on causality and discursive reasoning in his investigative and therapeutic interventions, Coltrera suggested that the legacy of these traditional influences on current analytic practice includes the slighting of preoedipal and nonverbal determinants and the concentration on manifestations of dynamic phenomena in the present. Focusing on the ongoing features of the transference tends to equate working through with the elucidation of patterns of wish and defense as they currently appear, to the neglect of an understanding of the genetic antecedents of the instinctual components of transference resistances.

October 16, 1978. SYMBOLIC PROCESSES AND SYMBOL FORMATION. Harold P. Blum, M.D.

To help clarify the term "symbolism" and to more rigorously differentiate between the two main symbolic processes—unconscious or psychoanalytic symbolism and the symbolism involved in receptive and expressive language and related phenomena—Dr. Blum made the following points. Unconscious or psychoanalytic symbolism is related to the primary process and is not taught or learned. A universal phenomenon, it appears spontaneously during development, unconnected with any intention to communicate with another, and promotes fantasy rather than reality testing. Psychoanalytic symbols arise out of early perceptions of the body and its functions which are primarily but not exclusively visual, are connected with infantile instinctual aims and their objects, and are linked by a process of perceptual association through a series of displacements away from the body to more distant and neutral percepts. Psychoanalytic symbols are idiosyncratic and are not bound by social custom or convention. They convey disguised thoughts and affects which are outside of awareness and may be viewed as representing compromise formations between instinctual wishes and their gratification. Communicative symbolism or language, as distinguished from psychoanalytic symbolism, is related to the secondary process. It is learned and taught, is intended for communication with others, is not idiosyncratic but consensually shared, has its origins primarily in auditory-vocal percepts generated by the self and important objects, and promotes reality testing.

Absolute distinction between psychoanalytic symbolism and linguistic symbolism is an idealization: inevitably, neither will appear in pure form wthout some admixture of the other. Both probably evolve from an undifferentiated symbolic-cognitive matrix and then develop along relatively independent lines, with unconscious symbolism primarily a drive derivative and linguistic symbolism chiefly associated with autonomous ego function. During the course of their parallel development, the two basic types of symbolic processes overlap and blend; thus their functions are not as clearly demarcated as formal definitions would suggest. Linguistic symbols are most often considered to subserve adaptation, while unconscious symbols are thought to promote fantasy and drive gratification. But unconscious symbolism plays a major role in ego development, particularly in the development of sublimation. Regression in the service of the ego, in which unconscious symbolism may contribute to wit and literature, represents another adaptive function of unconscious symbolism.

Sara Vogel  

DISCUSSION: Concerning the precursors of the two symbolic processes during the first year, Dr. Annemarie P. Weil pointed out that infants' preverbal gestures and their understanding of symbols used by others in asking questions of, suggesting things to, and naming things for them may be considered as antecedents of linguistic symbol formation. The fluidity and frequent misunderstanding of

357

early speech development may have an effect on the formation of later unconscious symbols. Dr. Weil stressed the great individual differences among children in degrees of freedom and richness of both conventional representational play and of idiosyncratic symbolic play. She emphasized the importance of the child's interaction with the mother in the formation of both types of symbolism, pointing out that maternal feedback in the form of repetition, refinement, and clarification enhances the child's linguistic repertoire. Dr. Melvin A. Scharfman felt that the distinction between psychoanalytic symbolism and linguistic and other symbolic processes should not be overdrawn. He noted that the unconscious signified and signifier are bound to one another in a manner usually associated with secondary process thought. This suggests that unconscious symbols partake more of secondary process than a definition strongly linking them with primary process would indicate. Dr. Scharfman contrasted the early memories which Freud referred to as "perceptual images" with more complex "memory images" which are organized according to the secondary process. Early "perceptual images" seem related to psychoanalytic symbols and appear in dreams and hallucinations. Freud abandoned the idea that memory traces differ in location in the psychic apparatus and instead proposed that shifts in energic cathexis would determine the accessibility to consciousness of a given memory trace. Certain people, such as artists, may become conscious of psychoanalytic symbols; or secondary process manifestations, such as word representations, may become subjected to the primary process. This fluidity, as it affects the accessibility to awareness and the type of thinking associated with memory traces, illustrated Dr. Scharfman's contention that sharp distinctions between psychoanalytic symbolism and linguistic symbolism should be tempered. Dr. Henry Edelheit suggested that the term "unconscious symbolism," used by Dr. Blum, is misleading since it may refer to the unconscious meanings associated with play, with language, and with elements in dreams, fantasies, and symptoms. A better term to designate the symbolism of the unconscious might be Lilli Peller's term "primordial symbolism." Dr. Edelheit pointed out that, although Dr. Blum attributed the universality of "primordial symbolism" to the commonality of developmental experiences for all children, the uniformity of children's experiences does not appear to be as great as the uniformity of symbols. He felt, therefore, that further explanation for this uniformity was needed and suggested the hereditary transmission of a set of limits and potentials for image formation.

Pollock reviews the literature concerning the specificity concept of psychosomatic illness. He presents data which seem to indicate that specificity was at one time very implausible: namely, data were produced which suggested that specificity does not exist in regard to psychosomatic illness. A Preliminary Report of a Case of Consummated Mother-Son Incest. Marvin Margolis. Pp. 267-293.

James Bing

James Bing

James Bing  

Margolis describes a case of mother-son incest in which the individuals were in psychotherapy for nine years. He suggests that the frequency of such cases is greater than we have heretofore recognized. His explanation for this is that countertransferences and embarrassment on the part of the individuals involved cause the phenomenon to be suppressed or repressed. He discusses the relationship of the sexual impulse to the enormous aggressive drive that these patients have; in fact, the act itself may well represent more an expression of the aggressive drive than the sexual drive. This is further illustrated by frequent examples of the stabbing of mothers by sons which has obvious symbolic incestuous implications.

October 11, 1976. SEPULCHRAL ART AND THE TRANSITIONAL EXPERIENCE: ETRUSCAN BURIAL SYMBOLS. Simon A. Grolnick, M.D.

Dr. Grolnick suggested that sepulchral art and its symbols lend themselves to an interpretation based on Winnicott's concept of the transitional object. According to Dr. Grolnick, the transitional object functions to stabilize self/object, awakening/sleeping, and concrete/abstract polarities, and this is developmentally related to humanity's persistent attempts to bridge the interface between life and death with burial art and symbols. A complex continuum exists between the bedtime rituals of children and the rituals and art complementing a culture's burial practices. Children use the comforting transitional object to allay the separation anxiety evoked by sleep and, later, by the idea of death.

March 13, 1979. SECRETS, ALLIANCES AND FAMILY FICTIONS: SOME PSYCHOANALYTIC OBSERVATIONS. Theodore J. Jacobs, M.D.

Dr. Jacobs presented material from two analytic cases to illustrate a subject seldom mentioned in the literature: the impact of individual secrets and secret alliances within the family on the development of individual pathology. Some of the secrets concern facts that must be concealed; others are fictitious and constitute family myths; all, however, serve to regulate the degree to which communication is possible.

The first case was that of a young woman whose feelings about her present analyst and about her previous analyst were a secret. These feelings reflected her secret feelings about her father and her stepfather which had been driven underground by her mother's behavior. Her positive feelings for her father had been hidden from her stepfather and mother. Her fantasies about her former analyst re-enacted another family secret: her mother's longing for her father, which was denied by the mother but was apparent to the patient and remembered through identification with her mother. Dr. Jacobs noted that exploration of the transference secret opened the way for recovery of other secrets. He also noted that secrets can serve as "screen experiences." The second patient, a middle-aged woman, had significant amnesia for adolescence as well as for early childhood. Her inability to remember reflected not only her own defensive operations but also those of every member of her family. Her parents felt a need to forget the Holocaust. Her father fictionalized his early life to ward off the memory of early traumas while her mother attempted to blot out several important losses and depressive episodes. The analysis of a screen memory and a piece of acting out allowed for the reconstruction of the patient's past. Although she thought the reconstruction was valid, it was not useful until verified by her mother.

Dr. Jacobs, extrapolating from the case material, pointed out that the existence of secrets and collusions within the family interferes with the optimum development of the following ego functions: memory, perception, integration, judgment, the sense of reality, and certain aspects of the synthetic function. Learning is also affected. The family secret has a stimulating effect on libidinal and aggressive drives. This can lead to extensive use of repression, suppression, and denial which further affect memory. Dr. Jacobs suggested that "forgotten secrets act as one category of repressed memories, which, because of the intensity and condensation of the drive derivatives associated with them, require a corresponding intensity of repressive forces to keep them from conscious awareness. It is partly for this reason too that the tendency to act out such secrets is so strong." Dr.

Mothers, Fathers, and Children. Explorations in the Formation of Character in the First Seven Years

By Sylvia Brody and Sidney Axelrad. New York: International Universities Press, Inc., 1978. 669 pp.

Edward Schiff

Edward Schiff

Edward J. Schiff
CLEVELAND

Edward Schiff  

This comprehensive book is a longitudinal study of the relationship between forms of parental care and the psychological development of the child. It is a follow-up of these authors' research on the behavior of infants in the first year of life.1 In the earlier study Brody and Axelrad hypothesized that it is possible to construct a typology of nurturing in the first year of life and to predict that the quality of mothering will be reflected in the infant's development; the more adequately mothered infants will have a smoother and better development compared to the less adequately mothered ones. Using clinical ratings and various statistical profile analyses, they concluded that these hypotheses were borne out for their sample of one hundred thirty-one mothers and infants.

In the present work, the authors report on the same babies (and mothers—and some fathers) through the seventh year of childhood. The current study began when the oldest infants in the previous study reached the age of four and the youngest, two.

The raw research data of the current volume consist of direct observation of mothers, fathers, and children, as well as sophisticated objective tests at different developmental stages, school visits, and exhaustive analyses of the drawings of the children at ages four to five. Many inferences about psychic processes are drawn from the theoretical and clinical interpretations of the data.

[[RunningHead]]

Hysteria: The Elusive Neurosis. (Psychological Issues, Vol. XII, Nos. 1/2, Monograph 45/46.)

By Alan Krohn, Ph.D. New York: International Universities Press, Inc., 1978. 343 pp.

Richard Isay

Richard Isay

Richard A. Isay
NEW YORK

Richard Isay  

Most analysts view traditional psychiatric nosology as too simplistic or obscure. By approaching psychopathology dynamically, however, they sometimes sacrifice both the parsimony and shared vocabulary

538

that is so useful, for example, in teaching medical students and psychiatric residents. In his book Alan Krohn attempts to clarify the diagnosis of hysteria by bringing a "psychoanalytic approach to bear on the hysterical personality and the hysterical neurotic." He demonstrates how we may arrive at a diagnosis of hysterical neurosis, character, and personality that is systematic and also organizing and synthesizing of psychoanalytic observations. Making use of the concepts of unconscious conflict, ego structure, cognitive style, defense, resistance, and intrapsychic and interpersonal conflict, his approach is both detailed and extensive.

The monograph is divided into chapters on Freud's Theory of Hysteria, Definitions of Hysteria, Historical and Cross-Cultural Perspectives, Comprehensive Definition and Case Illustration, and Concluding Remarks. The review of Freud's theory and the further historical review of the many definitions of hysteria are meticulous and scholarly.

Particularly valuable is the author's attempt to clarify and elucidate hysteria in men, which has been variously diagnosed as passive-aggressive, passive-dependent personality disorder, narcissistic character disorder or even depressive neurosis. It would, however, be a mistake and a misreading to view this monograph simply as a definitional study of hysteria, for it is also a study of the methodology of diagnosis from a psychoanalytic perspective.

The author views the hysteric as having intrapsychic conflicts that are "essentially oedipal," and he sees the preoedipal material that emerges during the course of an analysis as being primarily of a regressive or resistance nature. Although Krohn acknowledges that preoedipal traumata shape and change the nature and structure of the oedipal relationship, he feels that the analysis must focus on the nature of the oedipal conflict, on which he believes the definition of hysteria rests.
