The Psychiatric Foundation of Medicine

Edited by George U. Balis, Leon Wurmser, Ellen McDaniel, and Robert G. Grenell. Vol. I: Dimensions of Behavior; Vol. II: The Behavioral and Social Sciences and the Practice of Medicine; Vol. III: Basic Psychopathology; Vol. IV: Clinical Psychopathology; Vol. V: Psychiatric Clinical Skills in Medical Practice; Vol. VI: Psychiatric Problems in Medical Practice. Boston and London: Butter-worths Publishers, Inc., 1978.

H. Blank

H. Blank

H. Robert Blank
WHITE PLAINS, N.Y.

H. Blank  

This formidable work was written specifically as a textbook for medical students (a paperback edition is available) and physicians. The editors, justifying it on the basis of its comprehensive scope, state that "it contains the contributions of all the disciplines that are relevant to the behavioral, psychological, social, and humanistic

540

aspects of medicine, as well as the contributions of clinical psychiatry." The six volumes are organized in an evolving sequence, each presenting a progression of concepts as the student progresses through medical school.

The editors are right: this is a work of excellent quality, useful to medical students, psychiatrists, and the many psychoanalysts actively involved in teaching medical students and training psychiatrists. It would be more useful if Volume VI had a cumulative index, an omission that can be corrected in the second edition. Each volume does have a more than adequate index.

Given the scope of the text and the large number of authors representing many disciplines, it is surprising that so few of the contributions are deficient. In fact, the bulk of them range from very good to superb.

Psychoanalysis is well represented. With one exception, the lists of contributors do not indicate who are psychoanalysts. I identified the following as psychoanalysts, in addition to Wurmser and McDaniel: Eugene B. Brody, Hilde Bruch, George L. Engel, Robert Gibson, Ghislaine D. Godenne, Herbert S. Gross, Peter Hartocollis, John D. Rainer, Jon A. Shaw, and Julian L. Stamm. Wurmser's numerous contributions deal lucidly with many psychoanalytic topics, highlighting the importance of psychoanalysis in psychiatry.

The first two chapters in Volume I deserve special praise. "The Need for a New Medical Model: A Challenge for Biomedicine" by Engel (reprinted from Science, 196: 129-136, 1977) is an elegant exposition of the author's biopsychosocial model. It is based on an incisive critique of the present medical model which, loaded as it is with conceptual straitjackets, is still loudly prescribed for psychiatry by many psychiatrists and other physicians.

Psychoanalytic Study of the Child. XXXII, 1977

Depressive Affect. T. L. Dorpat. Pp. 3-27.

Ways of conceptualizing depressive affect (as distinct from depressive illness) form the body of this complex and rich paper. Four aspects are presented: classification, developmental line, the role of depressive affect in adaptation, and its role in formation of symptoms and defenses. Two primary affects of unpleasure are postulated, "primary anxiety affect" and "primary depressive affect." Secondary derivatives of the latter include helplessness, hopelessness, depressive affect per se, shame, guilt, grief, sadness, and mourning. Depressive affect can be distinguished from primary anxiety by specific criteria. The degree of experienced certainty differentiates them. The developmental line from a state of infantile helplessness (requiring no time sense) to hopelessness (requiring considerable representational and synthesizing work to be experienced) is outlined thus: helplessness, shame, depressive affect and guilt, and finally sadness, grief, and mourning. In adaptation the reciprocal relationship between affective and structural development is emphasized. An effective ego and superego are necessary to master depressive affect. Conversely, depressive affect is necessary to the development of ego and superego.

Israel Annals of Psychiatry and Related Disciplines. XVI, 1978

A Model for an Alternative Educational/Treatment Program for Adolescents. S. Schneider. Pp. 1-20.

Schneider offers a model for a comprehensive therapeutic program for adolescents whose psychopathology is such that they need to be removed from the family and social environment and obtain treatment that will enable them to begin to utilize peer and adult relationships and maintain and sustain psychological growth. Basic concepts essential to the understanding of the residential treatment process are presented and explained. The program is a unique educational/vocational/recreational/psychological one that attempts to provide treatment through "process," utilizing a combination of psychological and group social work theory with a psychiatric base. A combination of half-way house, residential treatment center, and therapeutic community/milieu in a family-style setting serves as the impetus for growth. Students are far removed from the pathogenic family nexus and are provided with appropriate, consistent, external controls. Elements of the treatment program and its essential facilities, goals, and philosophy are examined. Included also is an evaluation, a follow-up, and a discussion of an American population merged with an Israeli one.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Israel Annals of Psychiatry and Related Disciplines. XVI, 1978

The Influence of Various Therapeutic Milieus on the Course of Group Treatments in Two Groups of Soldiers with Combat Reaction. M. Ben-Yakar; H. Dasberg; I. Plotkin. Pp. 183-195.

The sudden outbreak of the Yom Kippur War in 1973 and the very acute transition from an affluent and peaceful environment to conditions of full-scale war called for a rapid reorganization of psychiatric services to cope with the many cases of acute war neurosis and mental breakdown in combat. Large teams of psychiatrists and clinical psychologists, most of them civilians until the moment of war, began to work within a military framework. Exposed to unusual war stresses and clinical demands, these clinicians had to cope with their own responses while at the same time having to modify previously widely-accepted methods of treatment or to improvise and create new ones. Two clinical teams are described in the paper. They showed complex psychosocial reactions to acutely changing conditions, thereby bringing into existence divergent types of therapeutic milieus. One of these favored pharmacological means of support and abreaction. The other milieu accentuated the psychodynamic aspects of group interactions. Soldiers with combat breakdown who joined these milieus readily adopted the sets of expectations and treatment aims inherent in these clinical environments. The divergent courses of psychodynamic and clinical developments in two groups of soldiers attached to these two different therapeutic milieus are compared through analysis of the group processes during short-term, intensive, and dynamically oriented group therapy. Long-term outcomes are not compared. Some conclusions are drawn pertaining to the organization of psychiatric teams and group treatments in future times of war stress. Civilian systems of delivery of mental health services may derive benefit from the observations described here.

Literature and Psychology. XXVIII, 1978

The Popular Meaning of Chaucer's "Physician's Tale." Thomas L. Kinney. Pp. 76-84.

Although generally popular, Chaucer's "Physician's Tale" has always seemed of inferior literary merit. Previous critical thought is reviewed. The paradox can be understood by applying dream analysis technique. The tale is seen as an adolescent girl's response to the claims of sexuality in conflict with the urge for

346

parental security. The solution here is a denial of sexuality presented as an erotic death at the hands of the father. The dream-tale is compared to Campbell's consideration of rites of passage as calls to adventure accepted or refused; here the refusal of the call culminates in death. Chaucer opened to the conscious level unconscious patterns recognizable by a popular audience. The high interest in this tale in certain periods of the Middle Ages may have been related to preoccupation with reproduction as good and death as evil because of the impact of the plagues on population levels.

Meetings of the Psychoanalytic Association of New York

March 19, 1979. PANEL DISCUSSION: INSIGHT IN CHILD AND ADULT PSYCHOANALYSIS. Harold Blum, M.D., Peter A. Neubauer, M.D., and Samuel Abrams, M.D.

Dr. Blum emphasized the central position of insight in psychoanalysis, noting that it is inseparable from analytic theory, technique, and therapeutic effect. Insight propels the analytic process forward, creating a circular interaction between further insight and productive analytic work leading to structural change. Insight, however, also occurs outside of analysis, as demonstrated by the extraordinary illuminations of the human condition which occur in art. In psychotherapy insight tends to be superficial, selectively used, and limited to current derivatives of unconscious conflict, as opposed to its use in analysis where it reaches and resolves unconscious conflicts in a far more pervasive and enduring way.

Insight into preconscious problems achieved by clarification and education is not comparable to analytic insight, in which systematic interpretation deals with renewed resistance and is followed by working through, continued analytic work, and further extension of insight. Assimilation of insight is usually gradual and tenuous until it is confirmed and recreated in the wealth of interlacing analytic data. The analytic process proceeds with increasing insight into the unconscious pathogenic childhood conflicts and their later derivatives and effects. While insight is central to analytic progress it can, as Kris noted, be used for purposes of defense or infantile gratification. Additionally, intellectualization can take the place of insight, producing pseudo-insight. The "good hour" has been "prepared" unconsciously by the preceding analytic work and culminates in new autonomous insights which in turn are integrated into the personality, largely out of awareness, and contribute to the autonomy of other ego functions.

Although most analysts would agree that the goal of analysis is insight, this view has occasionally been challenged.

A Transference Dream with Superego Implications

Wayne Myers M.D.

Wayne Myers

Wayne A. Myers, M.D.
1385 York Avenue (Apt. 17G)
New York, N.Y. 10021

Wayne Myers  

ABSTRACT

A type of transference dream is described in which the male analyst is transformed into a woman. For male patients, this transformation of the threatening father-analyst into the protective maternal figure appears to mitigate the threat of castration for incestuous oedipal wishes. For female patients, the substitution of the maternal figure seems to serve as a wishful undoing of narcissistic mortifications to the young girl's emerging sense of femininity and sexuality suffered at the father's hands during the oedipal years. Maternal and paternal contributions to superego formation are discussed, as is the relative importance of oedipal narcissistic traumata and penis envy.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Dorothy Burlingham—1891-1979

Hansi Kennedy

Hansi Kennedy

Hansi Kennedy  

Dorothy Tiffany Burlingham died on November 19, 1979, in London in her eighty-ninth year. Because she was an unusually modest and unassuming person, her work and contributions to psychoanalysis may not be as widely known as they deserve. Her professional life as a psychoanalyst spanned more than fifty years and was intimately linked with the earliest days of child psychoanalysis in Vienna and with the work of Anna Freud of whom she was a close friend and collaborator throughout these years.

As one of the daughters of the famous New York artist and jeweler, Charles Tiffany, she grew up, married, and lived in the United States until she moved to Vienna in 1925 to seek analytic help. She had a short period of analysis with Theodor Reik before he moved to Berlin and was then analyzed by Freud himself. This gradually developed into a training analysis, and she eventually became a member of the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society at a time when the other young members included Anna Freud, Ernst and Marianne Kris, Edward and Grete Bibring, Heinz Hartmann, Richard Sterba, and Robert Waelder, to mention just a few.

Her interest in child analysis and its application to education also first stemmed from personal needs. Her four young children were in psychoanalytic treatment, and she felt that the conventional Viennese schools did not meet their requirements. She resolved this problem by founding a small modern school, engaging as teachers two young men who later acquired renown in the psychoanalytic world: Erik Erikson and Peter Blos. Excited by this venture, she wanted to spread the knowledge of psychoanalytic ideas to other educators and, with Anna Freud, set up the first psychoanalytic seminars for nursery school teachers in Vienna.

Dreaming and Memory. A New Information-Processing Model

By Stanley R. Palombo, M.D. New York: Basic Books, Inc., 1978. 237 pp.

Leon Altman

Leon Altman

Leon L. Altman
NEW YORK

Leon Altman  

This is a book whose aim, the author says, is to go beyond the traditional psychoanalytic theory of dreams as formulated by Freud. Palombo wishes to "enlarge" this theoretical framework by allowing "the research findings of dream physiology and the recent contributions of information theory and cognitive psychology to fit comfortably within it, not to mention the work of the dream physiologists who have labored all along outside the theoretical boundaries set by Freud and his direct successors in the psychoanalytic world" (p. 10). The author has formulated a new model for the function of dreaming, which, whether or not it may "fit comfortably" within Freud's theoretical framework, translates the language of psychoanalysis into terms compatible with information theory. Palombo concedes that those unfamiliar with information theory—this reviewer is one such—will be substantially assisted in understanding his thesis if they are conversant with the work of others in this field (he mentions Peterfreund and Rosenblatt and Thickstun).

The model is based upon the assumption of the existence of a permanent associative memory structure or "tree." From the beginning of life, experiential information is stored in "adaptively suitable" locations within this memory structure.

[[RunningHead]]

The Psychoanalytic Study of Society. VII, 1976

Superego Development and Psychopathology. Daniel M. A. Freeman; Edward F. Foulks; Patricia A. Freeman. Pp. 107-122.

In this first of several articles, the authors outline the theoretical framework upon which their future articles will be based. It is an overview of the development of the superego from its earliest precursor through the vicissitudes of the separation-individuation process and the oedipal period. The authors follow Margaret Mahler's stages of separation-individuation, meticulously depicting the components in each stage relating to superego formation. The earliest primordia of the superego become established during the symbiotic phase. Motor prohibitions and preverbal communications from the parent become internalized in memory traces which establish the basis for the first patterns of impulse control. An important component in this process is the angry look of the parental eye which may contribute to the later development of the sense of shame. In the differentiation, practicing, and rapprochement subphases, the task of integrating the images of "good" and "bad" mother as well as "good" and "bad" self is to be accomplished. The ego ideal, originating from the blissful state of union of the symbiotic phase, undergoes successive stages of development parallel to those of the superego precursors. At the time of the oedipal resolution, the ego ideal and the superego precursor fuse to form the superego proper with its functions of positive and negative sanctions.

Dying. A Psychoanalytic Study with Special Reference to Individual Creativity and Defensive Organization

By Tor-Björn Hägglund. Helsinki: Psychiatric Clinic of the Helsinki University Central Hospital, 1976, 138 pp.; New York: International Universities Press, Inc., 1978. 259 pp.

George Pollock

George Pollock

George H. Pollock
CHICAGO

George Pollock  

We all live under a death sentence throughout our lives, although the form, shape, and means of dealing with this threat to our existence varies from person to person. Until the early 1960's few papers and monographs by psychoanalysts were devoted to this enigmatic, inevitable, and universal topic. Theologians and philosophers have long addressed the theme of death and immortality. Painters, writers, sculptors, composers, poets, have all creatively depicted aspects of this human anxiety, but systematic studies of the phenomena and experiences were few. Then came the "death and dying" movement, particularly in the United States and Great Britain. Much of this research, clinical as well as conceptual, was based on the classic contributions of Freud (e.g., Mourning and Melancholia and On Transience) and brought a neglected area to our awareness. The thanatologic had been avoided and denied for many internal and external reasons. Now taboos could be faced and observed directly. Theoretical formulations were offered about stages of dying, bereavement, and grief work. The hospice movement came to the United States, and one began to read about "preventive intervention" in the dying-bereavement process. In extreme situations one could but wonder about the possible risk involved if preparations for death were pursued too vigorously. Suggestion and voodoo death are powerful agents, and now that it has been posited that underlying biological mechanisms account for their action, it is conceivable that one could hasten the dying-death process if one were too active in preparing the unfortunate for the inevitable fate that awaits us all.

Other investigations into related, connected, and derivative areas have followed: for example, studies of the mourning-liberation process and adaptation, pathological mourning processes, suicide, anniversary phenomena, object loss at various stages of the life span, the relationship of the process of liberation from mourning to creativity, to name but a few. The separation of object loss from the mourning-liberation processes was important because of the linkage, previously seen as tight, which had prevented the investigation of these two different phenomena until they could be researched independently.

The World of Emotions. Clinical Studies of Affects and their Expression

Edited by Charles W. Socarides, M.D. New York: International Universities Press, Inc., 1977. 625 pp.

Anton Kris

Anton Kris

Anton O. Kris
BROOKLINE, MASS.

Anton Kris  

This volume is a collection of thirty-one psychoanalytic papers, published between 1927 and 1972, each with a brief commentary by the editor and chosen principally to illustrate "the clinical manifestations of specific affects" (p. 3). Socardies tells us in the Introduction that his interest in compiling this anthology began with the preparation of his 1966 paper, "On Vengeance," which appears on pages 403-425 of this volume. "Articles on depression, bitterness, arrogance, boredom, enthusiasm, envy, gratitude, jealousy, and querulousness were of great relevance to the formulation of the psychodynamics of vengeance, helping me to clarify my concepts and casting light on various facets of the problem, and led to my paper 'On Disillusionment: The Desire to Remain Disappointed' (1971)" (p. 2). The 1971 paper is also included in this volume and begins:

Psychoanalysis, in penetrating the intricacies of ego psychology, has turned increasingly to the study of affects. These involve the whole personality, resulting in chronic ego states, thereby inducing the ego to cope not only with underlying conflicts but also with the initiating affect. Affects constitute severe blocks to our therapeutic endeavors and must be treated as strong resistances in order to uncover the infantile material. They loom prominently in the working-through process of successful psychoanalytic therapy (pp. 554-555).

The aim of this volume is to illustrate "the multiple clinical aspects of affective life and the myriad forms of their expression" (p. 6). Socarides has succeeded in his aim. The papers, true to his subtitle, are mainly clinical descriptions, many with fine, detailed accounts of analytic experience. A broadly diverse group of affects is considered seriatim, from a number of points of view, inviting comparison and contrast not only among the affects described but among the clinical and theoretical styles of the authors.

The majority of affects examined in this book belong to the "unpleasure" group, in Brenner's useful formulation,1 with considerable overlap among them. Many of the contributions refer to severe illness, with extreme trauma early in life. But love and enthusiasm are here, too, and, more important, compassionate understanding.

Ralph R. Greenson—1911-1979

Albert Solnit

Albert Solnit

Albert Solnit  

Ralph Greenson died on November 24, 1979, at the age of sixty-eight after a life of great personal and scientific fulfillment. A leading member of his generation of psychoanalysts, Romi Greenson, as most of us called him, was a man of many parts who was devoted to his family, his patients, and his students.

Greenson was fiercely committed to the advancement of psychoanalytic theory and practice. He considered himself a link between the pioneers of psychoanlysis in the United States and the post-World-War-II generation of psychoanalysts. He thoroughly enjoyed being on the scene with Hartmann, Kris, and Loewenstein, serving on the Board on Professional Standards of the American Psychoanalytic Association with Max Gitelson, and having conversations about psychoanalytic practice with Ernest Jones. His friendships with Max Schur and Anna Freud grew out of such encounters. Romi Greenson was a clinical scientist and a romantic in the classical sense. He loved life in all of its aspects from infancy to old age and in its musical, poetic, artistic, and athletic expressions. He had a steady, unwavering concern for those who were about to succeed, those who failed, and those who were in pain, underprivileged, and in need.

Born September 20, 1911, in the melting pot of the Brownsville section of Brooklyn, a fraternal twin whose parents had come from Russia, Ralph Romeo Greenson grew up with his three siblings in the richly stimulating environment of a close family. He was born one half hour before his sister, Juliet. His mother, a pharmacist with a love for music and the arts, supported the family while his father studied to become a family physician.

American Journal of Psychiatry. CXXXV, 1978

The Psychodynamics and Developmental Psychology of the Borderline Patient: A Review of the Literature. Edward R. Shaprio. Pp. 1305-1315.

The author reviews the psychodynamics and developmental psychology of the borderline patient as described in the literature on intensive therapy, early mother-child interaction, and family interaction. Focusing on the borderline patient's characteristic difficulties in intimate relationships, he describes the patient's use of splitting and projective identification as seen in the characteristic transference-countertransference interaction in intensive therapy. These primitive defensive mechanisms, which are also utilized by family members, appear to contribute to a failure of empathic responses both during the child's early development and in the family interactions during the child's adolescence. The author concludes that conceptual attempts to relate adult and child phenomena, although highly speculative, create new and useful perspectives for the treatment of borderline patients.

Sigmund Freud. His Life in Pictures and Words

Edited by Ernst Freud, Lucie Freud, and Ilse Grubrich-Simitis; with a Biographical Sketch by K. R. Eissler. New York and London: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, Inc., 1978. 350 pp.

Leonard Shengold

Leonard Shengold

Leonard Shengold
NEW YORK

Leonard Shengold  

This book is a treasure for anyone who cares about Freud and his work. The visual images have a poignant evocative power, and they are accompanied by fragments, mostly Freud's own words, that make up a verbal miniature mosaic of an autobiography. Kurt Eissler's biographical sketch, beautiful and succinct, manages not only to outline Freud's life and character, but the development of his ideas as well. The photographs, familiar and unfamiliar, are for the most part reproduced very well on heavy paper. One can see (even in black-and-white) the power of the "terrible blue eyes" of Professor Brücke. One hauntingly lovely picture of the young Anna Freud ("my Antigone") would by itself justify owning this book (p. 275). Perhaps most moving of all is the sequence of photographs of Freud in his last years. These reflect the heroic stoicism of the old conquistador fighting the Nazis, the agony of his cancer, old age, and death. One sees the integrity in the face of the man who refused adequate sedation up to the day he died; who wrote, "I prefer to think in torment rather than not to be able to think clearly." The book's final pages have the transcendent tragic impact of Beethoven's last piano sonatas or of the late self-portraits of Rembrandt.

The Psychoanalytic Study of Society. VII, 1976

"Peter and the Wolf," A Musical Tale of Individuation and the Imagery of New Soviet Man: A Psychoanalytic Perspective on Russian Cultural History. Howard F. Stein. Pp. 31-64.

The musical tale is viewed as a metaphorical representation of Russian ethnopsychology, its conflicts, and their proposed Soviet resolution. Stein delineates essentials of the impact of history on the personality structure of the Russian people and the way they are represented by Prokofiev in his symphonic fairy tale. The Wolf, symbol of archaic orality, represents both the hordes of destructive enemies who invaded and devastated the land throughout its early history and the identification with those enemies embedded in the Russian psyche. The cautious and forbidding grandfather, paralyzed by his suspiciousness, is the "old" Czarist Russian image, while Peter is the new Soviet man. Peter tames rather than kills the wolf and takes him to Petrograd, the westernmost great city that looks toward the future aspirations of European civilization rather than the past of the Asian Steppe. An interesting analogy is drawn between the wolf of Prokofiev's creation and the wolf in Freud's Wolf Man's history.

[[RunningHead]]

The Trauma of Time. A Psychoanalytic Investigation

By Irvine Schiffer. New York: International Universities Press, Inc., 1978. 279 pp.

Martin Bergmann

Martin Bergmann

Martin S. Bergmann
NEW YORK

Martin Bergmann  

The psychology of time is a fascinating subject. The human being's ability to measure time objectively, structured around the earth's rotation, must be reckoned as one of the great achievements of the secondary process. Written history, economic development (the ability to measure labor objectively), and scientific progress are in turn all based on this achievement. Psychoanalytic case histories1 have demonstrated how very difficult it is for some to relinquish control over time to the objective world. Acknowledging the sovereignty of time is experienced as dangerous because it threatens the individual with the re-experiencing of early traumatic separations and the resurgence of sexual and aggressive wishes beyond the control of the ego. From such cases we realize how much narcissistic renunciation must have taken place before the concept of objective time was achieved.

Psychoanalysis deals primarily with subjective time. Time moves quickly in the good hour and slowly in depression and boredom. For some, analysis takes place outside of time; even the years of treatment become vague. Others must look at their watch during the hour, for they are afraid to relinquish time to the analyst. Poets have anthropomorphized time. Shakespeare says that "… never resting time leads summer on/To hideous winter, and confounds him there." And Milton rages against "blind fury with the abhorrent shears who slits the thin span of life." In this bitter literature about time Freud's little essay on transience2 stands out, for he believed that the limitation on the duration of any enjoyment raises the value of that enjoyment. Had eternal spring and youth been granted to us, as it was to the Olympian gods, we would not be able to cherish them the way we do. Freud concludes that we cannot enjoy the transience of beauty without the capacity to mourn.

Schiffer sees time as "the earliest target for liquidation," antedating and rivaling in significance the oedipus complex. The book could be subtitled "A Study in the Killing of Time.

Certainty: A Failed Quest

David Beres M.D.

David Beres

David Beres, M.D.
151 Central Park West
New York, N.Y. 10023

David Beres  

ABSTRACT

Can the quest for certainty ever succeed? The focus in this paper is on psychoanalytic considerations about certainty and on the issue of certainty within psychoanalytic theory and practice. The relation of certainty to truth, knowledge, and belief is discussed. The universal quest for certainty and the efforts to achieve it are examined; the uncertainties of science, including psychoanalysis, are emphasized.

Psychosomatic Disorders in Childhood

By Melitta Sperling, M.D. Edited and with Contributions by Otto E. Sperling, M.D. New York: Jason Aronson, Inc., 1978. 415 pp.

Lawrence Sabot

Lawrence Sabot

Lawrence M. Sabot
ROSLYN, N.Y.

Lawrence Sabot  

In a decade in which psychosomatic disorders are called psychophysiologic disturbances, when the psychiatric literature seems to indicate that psychoanalytic approaches to their treatment are outmoded, if not contraindicated, and when published studies emphasize possible physiologic mechanisms, biofeedback and behavior modification, it is perhaps timely that we are reminded of the ongoing interest that psychoanalysis has had in the poorly understood transitional area where the mental and the physical converge.

Psychosomatic Disorders in Childhood is not a definitive, balanced textbook as the title might suggest. It is a clinical psychoanalytic presentation of selected disturbances discussed emphatically from a defined, consistent point of view. The perspective employed is that of a busy, confident clinician interested in psychosomatic problems, an experienced psychoanalyst and child psychiatrist who was also a pediatrician and a teacher of psychoanalysis.

This work was edited after Melitta Sperling's death (in 1973) by her husband, Otto Sperling, who added a preface and three chapters. In its organization, Psychosomatic Disorders in Childhood is divided into: a preface; an introduction; and nine parts, which are in turn subdivided into twenty-five chapters.

[[RunningHead]]

The Problematical Self in Kant and Kohut

Richard Chessick M.D.

Richard Chessick

Richard D. Chessick, M.D.
636 Church St. Suite 628
Evanston, Ill. 60201

Richard Chessick  

ABSTRACT

Kant and Kohut each present an earlier and a later philosophical system. Each author bases his two systems on a conception of the self which is importantly different from the earlier system to the later system. The later systems are more or less incompatible with the earlier systems but have the advantage of elegance and explanatory power beyond the earlier systems. This recognition of a fundamental change in paradigm is mandatory in order to avoid confusion in hopelessly trying to reconcile the later system of Kohut with traditional psychoanalysis, and to render clear the fact that Kohut's psychology of the self in the broad sense represents a fundamental departure from classical psychoanalysis and Freud's psychodynamic theory, just as Kant's ethical philosophy cannot be reconciled with Kant's critical philosophy. Psychiatrists and psychoanalysts will have to make a choice.

[[RunningHead]]

The Oedipal Conflicts of the Analyst

Béla Grunberger

Béla Grunberger

Béla Grunberger
82, rue de l'Université
75007 Paris, France

Béla Grunberger  

ABSTRACT

A neglected dimension of the oedipus complex is the narcissistic aspect. The universal oedipal narcissistic injury linked to the developmental inadequacy of the child is crucially traversed only when optimal resolution of narcissistic cravings can be established. Rivalry with the parent of the same sex (the historic oedipus) is more visible than the profound oedipus linked to narcissistic injury. Failure to resolve the conflicts of the profound oedipus may have fateful consequences for the psychoanalyst himself. Some of the examples in this article are connected with the present situation of French psychoanalysis.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Edith Jacobson—1897-1978

Edward Kronold

Edward Kronold

Edward Kronold  

With the death of Edith Jacobson on December 8, 1978, at the age of eighty-one, psychoanalysis lost an outstanding clinician, a prolific writer, and a teacher of note.

Edith Jacobson was born in Hanau, a small town in the German province of Upper Silesia. She attended schools in Breslau and received her medical degree in Munich in 1924. (Her father had been a country doctor, and she had warm memories of going out on calls with him when she was a child.) In 1925, she went to Berlin to study psychiatry at the University in the department chaired by Professor Karl Bonhoeffer, and it was he who encouraged her to study psychoanalysis. She became a member of the Berlin Psychoanalytic Society in 1930 and was soon presenting papers which dealt with her interest in the problems of the superego and its development.

In the summer of 1938, Edith Jacobson arrived in New York, only a few short months after her release from a Nazi prison and her escape from Germany. How she came to be in trouble with the Nazis exemplifies her remarkable courage and loyalty. She had left Germany for the safe haven of Copenhagen where she had friends from Berlin. After she received news that a former patient was in trouble with the Nazis, however, she decided—against the warnings of her friends—to return to Germany to stand by her patient. She was soon arrested by the Gestapo and imprisoned for refusing to give information on the political activities of her patients. During her imprisonment, she acted as a kind of psychotherapist to the other inmates and made them the subject of a study which later appeared in print as "Observations on the Psychological Effect of Imprisonment on Female Political Prisoners" (1949).

She served two years of a three-year sentence and was then released because of a life-threatening thyrotoxicosis.

The Barren Prospect of a Representational World

Lawrence Friedman M.D.

Lawrence Friedman

Lawrence Friedman, M.D.
50 East 72nd St.
New York, N.Y. 10021

Lawrence Friedman  

ABSTRACT

This is a criticism of the view that the term "representation" has a peculiarly tangible clinical referent, a unique phenomenological meaning, and a special power to reveal subjective reality undistorted by theoretical constructs. Such a view is illegitimately encouraged by a tendency to think of "image" when we say "representation," even though we mean something more like "understanding," and by a tendency to treat understandings as though they were discrete experiences of the subject, rather than abstractions made by the observer. Because the reliance on representational terms mixes method with data, its covert principles of abstraction cannot be used to learn from new data.

Alan Eisnitz  

ABSTRACT

Units within the self-representation provide the quality for ego activity. The ego selects and cathects the appropriate unit of the self-representation. Oedipal identifications internalize the ego capacity to maintain the self-representation and its stability. Conflict can promote instability within the self-representation requiring special defenses to deal with the narcissistic stress. Such narcissistic conflict can arise at all levels of maturity.

ABSTRACT

Various meanings have been given to the word "metapsychology" by its opponents and proponents in the psychoanalytic literature. These are discussed and compared with the meaning Freud intended the word to have. The question of the place of psychoanalytic psychology in science—whether it is or is not a natural science—is also considered.

The Inner Space of the Body Image

Tor-Björn Hägglund M.D. and Heikki Piha M.D.

Heikki Piha

Tor-Björn Hägglund, M.D.
Heikki Piha, M.D.
Vesa PJA 665
91999 Oulu
Finland

Heikki Piha  

ABSTRACT

In a review of the psychoanalytic literature the authors show that throughout life the ego structure and identity of an individual are founded to a significant degree on the sensations and awareness of the body. It is suggested that psychic processes primarily evolve from cathecting biological events, of which the quality of rhythm seems to be most important. Each of the erogenous zones has its own inner space which is integrated into the body image and the body self as the child grows. The authors introduce the idea of the inner space of speech, voice, and respiration developing concurrently with the erogenous inner spaces. The most highly developed form is the adult genital inner space and its sublimated derivatives which form the basis for the biological creativity of begetting offspring and the psychic creativity of begetting original ideas.

On the Intrapsychic Function of Falling in Love

Martin Bergmann

Martin Bergmann

Martin S. Bergmann
1136 Fifth Avenue
New York, N.Y. 10028

Martin Bergmann  

ABSTRACT

Freud once planned a comprehensive "study of man's love life." Although only fragments of this project ever appeared in print, much of it can be reconstructed from Freud's letters and other sources. After tracing the evolution of Freud's thinking on this topic, the author proposes that there are five functions of the ego which are associated with falling in love. The bliss of falling in love is seen as the result of a revival of feelings that once belonged to the symbiotic phase of infancy. Other findings of Mahler are considered in terms of their significance for the understanding of love.

An Examination of Some Recent Criticisms of Psychoanalytic "Metapsychology"

Steven Ellman Ph.D. and Michael Moskowitz Ph.D.

Michael Moskowitz

Steven J. Ellman, Ph.D.
Doctoral Program in Clinical Psychology City University of New York
3332 Broadway
New York, N.Y. 10031
Michael B. Moskowitz, Ph.D.
277 West 10th St.
New York, N.Y. 10014

Michael Moskowitz  

ABSTRACT

Some of the recent criticisms of psychoanalytic metapsychology are discussed, particularly the contributions of Schafer and Rubinstein. An examination of the logic underlying these criticisms indicates that many of them are either 1) extratheoretical and say nothing about the scientific status of the theory or formulation under scrutiny; or 2) rely on certain a priori philosophical assumptions which, if adopted, would severely limit the scope of psychoanalytic theorizing. Several suggestions are offered which would allow for more fruitful discussion of substantive logical and empirical questions.

[[RunningHead]]

The Inner World. A Psycho-Analytic Study of Childhood and Society in India

By Sudhir Kakar. Oxford and New York: Oxford University Press, 1978. 213 pp.

J. Masson

J. Masson

J. Masson
BERKELEY, CALIF.

J. Masson  

Kakar's book is part of a growing, blatantly apologetic literature about India. The ancient Hindu world view is seen as coterminous with and equally valid as the Western scientific one. A studious attempt is made to avoid all judgments, and this extreme psychological relativism produces exactly what one expects: bland platitudes

333

and cautious generalizations that illuminate little except the author's schooling in an age of intellectual timidity.

Although Kakar is a trained psychoanalyst, the orientation he brings to his study of India is the Eriksonian psychosocial and epigenetic one which seems ever further removed from the concern with conflict that is at the center of classical psychoanalysis. Not surprisingly, Kohut's work is also invoked. To this reviewer, the power of these two systematic viewpoints to illuminate Indian (or any other) culture is limited.

Although the quality of this apology is higher than that variety which claims that Indian philosophy can enrich psychoanalysis, Kakar's position is little different. Since the Hindu world view is as good as any other, the objective scientist has only to describe it with sympathy and empathy to make a valid contribution to Western knowledge. I must point out that even if he is correct, Kakar should abstain from his endeavor, for he has neither the academic equipment for such an exploratory undertaking, nor the talents to redeem such purely descriptive accounts.

There are already innumerable descriptions of traditional Indian viewpoints in existence, and the one provided by Kakar falls well below the current standard. If this deficit were counterbalanced by a wide clinical experience, the book might have been redeemed. However, there are almost no references to Kakar's practice; thus the account he provides of the strains and strengths of Indian civilization rests or falls on the sophistication he is able to bring to bear on the accounts of others. This is a pity, for there is very little primary material about Indian analysands, and there certainly is place in this book for detailed descriptions of the cultural anomalies brought to light in the analyses of Indian patients.

The Role of the Superego in Exhibitionism. Marvin Glasser. Pp. 333-353.

Owen Renik

Owen Renik

Owen Renik  

The author draws upon his extensive experience in the treatment of patients who have been arrested for indecent exposure. He considers the need to defy a proscriptive superego a decisive etiological factor. In therapy, passive resistance and the urge to fail are the common picture, giving rise to resentment in the countertransference which can confirm the patient's proscriptive superego projections. The therapist needs to be clear that his goal is to analyze, not change behavior. In this way, a proscriptive attitude toward the patient can be avoided.

International Journal of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy. VII, 1978-1979

A Developmental View of Identifications Resulting from Maternal Impingements. Thomas H. Ogden. Pp. 486-507.

Owen Renik

Owen Renik

Owen Renik  

Patients who have been inadequately shielded from conflicted maternal feelings have the task of coping with the helplessness engendered by a premature awareness of the mother as separate. One consequence can be an identification with the conflicted aspect of the mother. Such an identification preserves the illusion of a satisfactory mother; it maintains an omnipotent fantasy of being the cause of mother's behavior, giving a reassuring sense of control; and it facilitates actual connection to a mother who may only attend to her child when the child's behavior is congruent with her own needs to project and externalize. Understanding that such an identification exists can help the therapist make sense out of an otherwise uncomfortable and bewildering set of countertransference reactions. Illustrative case material is presented.

Adolescent Sexuality in the Light of Group Processes

Otto Kernberg M.D.

Otto Kernberg

Otto F. Kernberg, M.D.
The New York Hospital—Cornell Medical Center Westchester Division
21 Bloomingdale Road
White Plains, N.Y. 10605

Otto Kernberg  

ABSTRACT

Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet is used to illustrate several connected theses regarding the relation of the couple to its surrounding social group: these include a couple's oedipal rebellion, the unconscious longing for and hatred of the idealized couple by the large group, the denial of aggression within the couple and its projection onto the group, the impotence of rationality and the conventionalization of sexuality in the large group, and the pervading dynamics of aggression in group formation. Pertinent psychoanalytic theories are briefly summarized, and this combined analysis is applied to the psychoanalyst's attitude regarding adolescent patients' love life.

[[RunningHead]]

Object Concept and Object Choice

Jacob Arlow M.D.

Jacob Arlow

Jacob A. Arlow, M.D.
120 West 59th St.
New York, N.Y. 10019

Jacob Arlow  

ABSTRACT

Any consideration of object relations theory and love requires a clear understanding of how the term, object relations, is used. In this contribution the concept of the object as a mental representation is emphasized. Developmentally, the evolution of the object cannot be separated from the vicissitudes of the drives. Sensorimotor experience is metaphorically assimilated in terms of pleasure-unpleasure components. Since the object concept develops in this context, it is inextricably linked to the vicissitudes of the drives. In later experience, these become organized in terms of persistent unconscious fantasies that ultimately affect object choice and patterns of loving. These are multiply determined and are influenced by contributions from all levels of development, predominantly integrated under the aegis of the oedipus complex.

Helen Gediman Ph.D. and Fred Wolkenfeld Ph.D.

Fred Wolkenfeld

Helen K. Gediman, Ph.D.
Fred Wolkenfeld, Ph.D.
400 West End Avenue
New York, N.Y. 10024

Fred Wolkenfeld  

ABSTRACT

In psychoanalytic supervision, supervisees manifest toward their supervisors many psychic patterns which parallel processes that are prominent in their interactions with their patients. The reverse influence is also observed: analyst and patient re-enact events of the supervisory situation. An expanded explanation for parallelism is offered which indicates how the structural and dynamic similarities of analysis and supervision link patient, analyst, and supervisor in a complex, multidirectional network that guarantees the emergence of this phenomenon.

Leon Balter M.D. , Zvi Lothane M.D. and James Spencer M.D.

Leon Balter, M.D.
55 East 87 St.

1435 Lexington Ave.

James H. Spencer, Jr., M.D.
10 East End Ave.
New York, N.Y. 10028

James Spencer  

ABSTRACT

Starting from certain unpublished remarks by Otto Isakower about "the analyzing instrument," we define it more precisely. The analyzing instrument has two constituents: a voluntary and controlled, situation-specific and goal-specific regressed state of mind in the analysand and a near-identical one of the same nature in the analyst. These parts function together through mutually evocative communication, leading to the elucidation of the analysand's unconscious fantasy-memory constellations.

Love, the Couple, and the Group: A Psychoanalytic Frame

Otto Kernberg M.D.

Otto Kernberg

Otto F. Kernberg, M.D.
The New York Hospital—Cornell Medical Center
Westchester Division
21 Bloomingdale Road
White Plains, N.Y. 10605

Otto Kernberg  

ABSTRACT

After a brief summary of previous work on the intrapsychic preconditions of love relations, this paper explores the built-in contradictions between the sexual couple and its social group, their mutual equilibrium, and the formation and dissolution of couples within the group. Clinical case material illustrates how three dimensions of love relations—namely, sexual experience, object relations, and superego integration—jointly determine a couple's stability within the social group. Finally, sexual psychopathology affecting the couple's interaction with its social group is explored in terms of some frequent pathological developments.

Toward a Critique of the Psychology of the Self

Arnold Rothstein M.D.

Arnold Rothstein

Arnold Rothstein, M.D.
300 Central Park West
New York, N.Y. 10024

Arnold Rothstein  

ABSTRACT

A critique of Kohut's "psychology of the self" is presented. This critique derives from the author's view that paradigm competition often unnecessarily polarizes and accentuates differences while obfuscating rather than facilitating communication. An attempt is made to delineate Kohut's valuable contributions and to integrate them within the structural hypothesis. In addition, a critique of a number of issues that are incompletely or "inexactly" elaborated within Kohut's paradigm is presented.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Four Fundamental Concepts of Psychoanalysis

By Jacques Lacan. Edited by Jacques-Alain Miller. Translated by Alan Sheridan. New York: W. W. Norton & Co., Inc., 1978. 290 pp.

Stanley Leavy

Stanley Leavy

Stanley A. Leavy
NEW HAVEN, CONN.

Stanley Leavy  

The translation into English of Lacan's writings and the publishing of critical and appreciative comment about them have at last reached the point at which interested psychoanalysts not familiar with the original French can come to informed first-hand opinions of Lacan's work. This volume is the first of the seminars conducted by Lacan to appear in English; it is actually the eleventh of the series, given in 1964, and published in France in 1973. Each seminar consists of a course of lectures, recorded on tape and then edited, which probably means that in printed form they have been fitted out with more logical connections than Lacan's oral style permits. Let the reader beware, however, if he or she hopes that the editor has domesticated Lacan; he has not. Each lecture is followed by a few questions from the floor, with replies by Lacan. The questions are asked by initiates into Lacan's concerns and vocabulary and consequently bear little resemblance to the questions that a newcomer would ask. There is a glossary, however, that is moderately helpful.

First of all, what are the "four fundamental concepts"? They are familiar ones: the unconscious, repetition, the transference, and the drive. More traditional analysts might propose other categories, but these are good enough. What Lacan does with them is another story. I believe that if there is one unifying assumption that will help us grasp the drift (here the most appropriate word) of Lacan's manipulation of these ideas, it is this: all psychoanalytic concepts, including these, must be understood with reference to the psychoanalytic situation itself.

526

[[RunningHead]]

Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XXXIX, 1975

Psychic Bisexuality. Materials for a Re-evaluation. Christian David. Pp. 695-856.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

This extensive study re-evaluates the concept of bisexuality in psychoanalytic theory, a concept constantly referred to but little understood and often relegated to the periphery of metapsychology, or even excluded entirely. It is an error to consider all bisexual manifestations as pathogenic or morbid; David stresses the organizing power of psychic bisexuality. It is a major concept, not a marginal one as some would hold. Although Freud never developed a clear and decisive theory of bisexuality, the concept was continually utilized and reaffirmed from 1899 to 1938. As a concept, it was present at the beginning of psychoanalysis, and it remained a major theoretical concept even after its dissociation from repression in 1914 and even after 1920, when the antagonism between Eros and the destructive instinct took precedence over all other previous oppositions and when reference to the phallic-castrated dichotomy became prevalent. It was a major theoretical concept even in Analysis Terminable and Interminable. Freud's ambiguity about the concept has been reflected in subsequent psychoanalytic writings, with opinions ranging from the view that bisexuality is fundamental to the psychoanalytic concept of man (Adler, Jung, Stekel, Groddeck, Ferenczi) to its pure and simple denial (Rado, Bergler, Sherfey).

Psychic bisexuality must be seen as a manifestation of the unconscious: the accent must be placed on the psychological rather than on the biological. Just as Freud early on noted the relative independence of psychology from biology in other instinctual matters, psychological bisexuality must be seen as developing upon biological bisexuality, but it must be recognized as eventually functioning independently of its biological foundation. According to David, the concept of bisexuality should undergo the same generalization in psychic life as the theoretical concept of sexuality. By so generalizing the concept we can discern the role of bisexuality in complex questions of sexual identity, in questions of primary and secondary identification, in questions of the distinction between masculinity and virility, between femaleness and femininity, etc.

Dream and Psychosis: Dream or Psychosis. Paul-C. Racamier. Pp. 173-193.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Racamier examines the relationship between madness and dreaming and suggests that the dream process and the psychotic process, even though they make use of neighboring and sometimes very similar pathways, actually run in contrary directions. He reviews previous work on the relationship between dreaming and madness and raises some interesting questions for authors who emphasize the similarities. Why, he asks, is dreaming sufficient for the majority of people? If

718

dreaming is the guardian of sleep, what does psychosis guard? Examining the literature on the dreams of psychotics, Racamier concludes that in actuality there is a failure of the function of dreaming and that the phenomena of psychosis are an extrusion of a dream that could not be dreamed. This view provides a key to understanding the resemblance as well as the opposition of the dream and the psychotic process. The psychotic is incapable of having a dream in the true sense. The schizophrenic, the author suggests, is something of an incarnation of a dream and lives the problematic but insistent existence of a dream.

719

A seventeenth-century case of demoniacal possession, that of Christoph Haitzman, is reviewed according to the original interpretation by Freud along the lines of libido theory (projection of repressed unconscious instinctual life). The case was reinterpreted by Fairbairn (1943) and Guntrip (1961), who conceptualized Haitzman's illness in terms of bad internalized objects. Taylor describes a patient he treated who felt possessed by demons. He concludes that both oedipal and preoedipal conflicts were involved and that successful treatment, which he describes, required integration and application of libido and object-relations theory.

ABSTRACT

Winnicott's thesis about transitional objects and transitional phenomena indicates that Kleinian theory, as well as his own preference for imaginative play with ideas, influenced his interpretation of his discovery and led to misapplications of its meaning. An alternative interpretation of its meaning, one that may be aligned more easily with other clinical data, is submitted. A brief review of the literature is appended.

Adolescent Psychiatry: Developmental and Clinical Studies. V, 1977

When and How Does Adolescence End: Structural Criteria for Adolescent Closure. Peter Blos. Pp. 5-17.

Although entry into adolescence is clearly demarcated by the somatic changes of puberty, the termination of this developmental phase is not clearly defined. The author seeks to establish criteria for defining the end of adolescence by describing the psychological tasks facing the late adolescent: the continuation and resolution of the oedipal conflict, particularly the negative (i.e., love for the parent of the same sex), the resolution of conflict over infantile traumata, and the achievement of ego continuity and a relatively stable character. He suggests ways in which one can recognize clinically both the healthy and the psycho-pathological resolutions of these adolescent tasks.

Roy Calogeras and Toni Alston

Toni Alston

Roy C. Calogeras
Dept. of Psychiatry (Box No. 4) U. S. Army Hospital Frankfurt
Giessener Str.
6 Frankfurt/M, Germany
Toni M. Alston
Universität Mainz Beratungsstelle für studentische Lebensfragen
Postfach 3980
65 Mainz, Germany

Toni Alston  

ABSTRACT

The main tenets of action language are summarized in an attempt to discern the direction in which psychoanalysis might go if action language becomes the "new metapsychology." The principal roots of action language are traced to the different linguistic/language and personality-and-culture models of anthropology and to the neobehaviorist currents of academic psychology. The authors' findings support the hypothesis that action language is a form of psychoanalytic behaviorism having idealism, logical positivism, and radical empiricism as its philosophical underpinnings. Its adoption would confound the entire motivational aspect of psychoanalysis. Specifically, the authors suggest that action language falls under the aegis of Wittgenstein's family of language games. When the action language game is said to be brought to a successful resolution, the language game disappears and, supposedly, so do the patient's conflicts.

The distinguished panelists whose papers will follow have each made important contributions to object relations theory, especially as viewed from the angle of love and the capacity for love in human relationships. Perhaps we might begin by asking why we are forced to speak separately of love and object relations. Does this parallelism of our scientific nomenclature confirm the criticisms that psychoanalytic theory has little to do with the elusive grandeur of love, the ecstasy of sexual passion, the gravity of the human condition, or the infinite subtleness of human relations? We cannot answer such questions today, but we hope to reconsider rigorously a number of recent, promising, and often confusing concepts in the sphere of object relations theory which have captured the center of our most recent clinical and theoretical literature.

Gilbert Rose  

Although the papers in this volume were originally delivered at symposia in May 1976, co-sponsored by the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis and New York University, most have already been published in either English or French. The book is divided into four sections: A Sociology of Psychoanalysis; Psychoanalysis; Creativity; and Psychoanalysis and Literature. Since themes often overlap, the papers will not necessarily be considered in sequence.

The first two, by Julien Bigras and François Péraldi, are polemical attacks on American psychoanalysis and ego psychology: for being conformist, dogmatic and authoritarian; for taming its candidates and manipulating its patients in submission to medical ideology; for over-theorizing on the one hand and devitalizing Freudian theory on the other, by discounting the death drives; for overestimating responsibility to the individual while seeking through technique to adapt the person to the complexity of his or her self and the accepted social order. In short, American psychoanalysis is counterrevolutionary and disregards its social and political responsibility by failing to understand, along with Hartmann, that reality is the battlefield of social classes, as already analyzed by Marx and Hegel.

This attack on American psychoanalysis runs concurrently with the discovery of the French Freud. Thus, one may suspect that France's sudden embrace of psychoanalysis, which followed their student riots of 1968, has less to do with psychoanalysis than with the French. That it is a complex social phenomenon is made clear in a thoughtful article by Sherry Turkle. Psychoanalysis is experienced by the French general public as a recent French discovery. It is seen as more radical, mature, and intellectual than that "perpetrated" by the United States.

Adolescent Psychiatry: Developmental and Clinical Studies. V, 1977

Psychoanalytic Perspectives on Adolescence, Psychic Development and Narcissism. Peter L. Giovacchini. Pp. 113-142.

In this rather complex, thought-provoking paper, Giovacchini addresses himself to two separate but related issues: 1) a definition of "narcissism" in adolescence, both pathological and healthy, and 2) approaches to the psychoanalytic treatment of people with severe narcissistic character pathology (not necessarily adolescent, although this form of pathology often manifests itself in adolescence). The author considers and compares Freud's and Melanie Klein's theories of infantile narcissism. He views pathological narcissism as the outcome of fixation at the prementational stages of early development when self and object world are not yet clearly differentiated. In adolescence, when character structure must be consolidated and the individual must adapt to the outside world, basic ego defects can no longer remain hidden. Symptoms then develop, such as rebellious acting out, confusion, attempts to simplify the outside world, sometimes psychosis. Giovacchini feels that, through classical psychoanalytic therapy which takes into account the need first to help the patient through prementational stages of relating, true ego growth can be promoted.

DISCUSSION: Dr. M. Donald Coleman emphasized that Dr. Galenson was attempting to relate clinical material from adult patients to the earliest phase of biphasic genital interest, a phase so early that distinct memories seem beyond recall. He felt that the clinical material presented, while strongly suggestive of pregenital derivation, could be better amplified if the author would describe her interpretations in greater detail so as to allow for a more dynamic understanding of their clinical impact. He stressed, however, that his own clinical experience also revealed the tenacity of women's sense of intellectual inferiority. Dr. Harold P. Blum expressed his reservations about the preoedipal "early genital phase" which was described. He felt that the dominant libidinal phase of the fifteen- to eighteen-month-old child is still the anal phase and the dominant anxiety still the fear of loss of the object and the object's love. He stated that for both men and women important examinations would characteristically evoke anxiety, guilt, and regression and that the reactions would depend upon the fixation points, traumas, and individual conflicts of each patient. Dr. Blum suggested the need for more clinical data to corroborate the validity of making a leap from the preoedipal rapprochement subphase to the adult female graduate student. He also wondered if the fact that Dr. Galenson's patients were self-selected or referred to her as a woman analyst might contribute to the cluster of common problems in this group.

[[RunningHead]]

Language and Interpretation in Psychoanalysis

By Marshall Edelson, M.D., Ph.D. New Haven: Yale University Press, 1975. 243 pp.

Henry Edelheit

Henry Edelheit

Henry Edelheit
NEW YORK

Henry Edelheit  

In this pioneering monograph Edelson hews away at the evertantalizing and elusive relationship between linguistics and psychoanalysis. Generally, he notes, language is transparent. We do not focus on it but see through it to the ideas, feelings, and images that it evokes. Like the peasant who was taught to read by Maxim Gorki, we should all feel wonder, as we scan the letters on a page, that we see not little black signs or marks, but a whole procession of images. To this transparency Edelson contrasts the opacity of language when we focus on it as an instrumentality, and on this opposition he brings to bear not only wonderment (like Gorki's peasant) but an array of sophisticated conceptualizations drawn from psychoanalysis, musicology, literary criticism, and more or less contemporary linguistic theory. I say more or less contemporary because new concepts have been developed so rapidly in linguistics that one can hardly apply them before they are well on the way to becoming at least partly obsolete. Some sort of treaty of limitations is needed to govern the conditions of rapidly proliferating interdisciplinary research.

Over the past twenty years Noam Chomsky's prolific writings have afforded a running commentary on his own shifting formulations. To a large extent, Edelson's application of these concepts reflects Chomsky's earlier versions. I mention this lest psychoanalytic readers turn to Edelson's book for an introduction to Chomskyan linguistics. For such a purpose they would do better to go to the source, and I would especially recommend the linguistic section of Language and Responsibility1 for a summary of the evolution of Chomsky's linguistic ideas from 1956 to the present. With this caveat in mind, Edelson's main points remain valid.

1Chomsky, N.: Language and Responsibility. New York: Pantheon Books, 1979.523

The interpretive role of the analyst is the central factor in the psychotherapeutic effect of psychoanalysis. The analyst's attitude of care and acceptance, reflected in the manner of his or her interpretations, is critical. Some patients in their communication have a greater capacity than others to work around the analyst's blind spots. This too aids the therapeutic process. Collusions between patient and analyst to protect the latter, usually based on a transference fantasy, are the most formidable impediments to analysis.

DISCUSSION: Dr. Milton Horowitz stated that sharing a secret is not necessarily pathogenic. The pathogenic factor is shared guilt. He suggested that "the sharing of a guilty secret makes every auditor an accomplice" and that the bearer of a secret often repeats the circumstances in the next generation. He noted that shared secrets enforce some loyalties, divide others. The analytic situation and the basic rule impose a conflict of loyalties on the analysand, who is the bearer of a secret. To keep a secret is often a way of holding onto old object ties, as well as keeping one's honor. To tell all to the analyst may be to unconsciously make the analyst an accomplice. Dr. Horowitz stated that analysands do not often simply reveal a family secret: the secrets may appear as disguised derivatives in dreams or as acting out. This is especially true for shared family secrets learned early in the child's life. Dr. Horowitz also noted how the secret tends to be sequestered from the associative connections in the analysis and may limit its effectiveness. Dr. Milton Jucovy discussed some additional groups of patients in whom secrets or family myths occur with great regularity. Adopted children comprise one such group. Another is the second generation of survivors of the Holocaust. Dr. Jucovy reported that because survivors do not often tell about their experiences, "offspring develop their own fantasies which may be pathological variants of the family romance theme." He cautioned that the pact of silence in the family may continue in the treatment situation, and this should be borne in mind by the analyst. Finally, Dr. Jucovy presented two interesting clinical illustrations in which the family secret concerned events prior to the birth of the patient or before the patient had sufficient cognitive ability to register it. He noted that failure to uncover the secrets may result in an incomplete or unsatisfactory analytic process.

American Journal of Psychiatry. CXXXV, 1978

The Social Context of Schizophrenia. J. K. Wing. Pp. 1333-1339.

During the past twenty-five years psychiatry has increased its understanding of the social context of schizophrenia in four major areas. Reasonable reliability can now be achieved in describing and recognizing many of the acute and chronic syndromes, so that comparability can be achieved between different research teams. Much is now known about the proximate social causes of symptoms and disabilities. The relationship between social and pharmacological treatments is now better understood. A more rational approach to the planning and prescription of services and to the counseling of patients and relatives can be made. Each of these lines of advance promises to lead to further progress in the future.

Journal of Psycholinguistic Research. VII, 1978

Language and Thought: Some Remarks on Chomsky and Piaget. Bärbel Inhelder. Pp. 263-268.

The author analyzes pertinent aspects of Piaget's and Chomsky's points of view on language and thought, indicating the similarities in their attempts to understand the underlying structures of both functions. The major difference between Chomsky and Piaget is that the latter considers all cognitive acquisitions, including language, to be the outcome of the gradual process of construction, whereas the former seems to be assuming as innate a general ability to synthesize the successive levels reached by an increasingly complex cognitive organization. Citing examples drawn from ongoing research in Geneva, the author also challenges Chomsky's assertion that there exist highly innate specific capacities which account for the principles underlying the development of scientific knowledge.
